subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
have a very few words to say on this bill, and I think it would be better to say them on the motion for second reading.
When the bill was in the resolution stage I referred to a press report of a statement alleged to have been made at the meeting of the bar association by the chief justice of the province of British Columbia in regard to judges' salaries. The chief justice of British Columbia advised me that he made no such statement. The item I read from the press is quoted in the letter that the chief justice wrote me, and reads as follows:
At the convention of the bar association at Banff, the statement was made by the chief justice of the province of British Columbia that salaries of judges are entirely inadequate and not in keeping with the dignity of superior courts.
The chief justice says that he did not make any such statement. He says that at the bar convention it was recommended by a special committee that the salaries of the puisne judges of the Supreme Court of Canada be increased to $25,000 a year, and that the salary of the chief justice be proportionately increased. On a motion to refer that report back, the chief justice, according to his letter, said that he did ask, not for any increase in judges' salaries, but that the salaries of superior court judges in the provinces should be brought more in line with those of the justices of the Supreme Court of Canada. That is the point that was made by the chief justice of British Columbia. Since he took the trouble to draw it to my attention, I thought I should bring it to the attention of the house.
Just one other word on the proposed increase in salaries mentioned in the bill. I emphasize only what I said when the bill was in the resolution stage. If I can make it any stronger than I made it then, I shall endeavour to do so. I do not believe it is anything short of a scandal that at this time we should be raising salaries that are of the proportions of supreme court judges' salaries, when hundreds of thousands of people throughout this country are being paid meagre salaries which are not going up but falling every day. I asked some questions on the unemployment situation in the dominion in the last two months as compared with the same period last year and I received figures which indicated that unemployment was approximately twice as great as it was last year. This means that twice as many people will be compelled to live on the meagre benefits from unemployment insurance. Because of that they will have to accept a lower standard of living. But here we are increasing salaries which in my opinion are already high enough.

Judges Act
The point made by the Minister of Justice when this matter was up for discussion before was that when they are appointed to the supreme court the judges are asked to give up certain things and perhaps make sacrifices by leaving their homes and taking smaller incomes than they received in the practice of their profession. I am not sure that there are not compensating factors for anything of that kind that may take place. The position of a justice of the supreme court is an honourable one. The honour itself is worth something, and the salary which goes with it is surely not inconsiderable. Not only is there the salary, but there is the pension. As long as they live, the justices of the supreme court receive a pension of two-thirds of their salary after they retire. When they die, one-third of that substantial pension goes to their widows. There are very few widows among the people with whom I associate who are left in that very fortunate position. I suggest to the House of Commons that if we want to improve the standard of living of the people of Canada we should begin at the bottom, and riot at the top.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can understand the attitude of the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Mac-Innis) and the ideas he has expressed. However, we are setting up a supreme court which is indeed to be the highest court in this land. If ever there was a time when we should endeavour to secure the best possible men for the bench, surely that time is now, when the supreme court has become the court of last resort.
I am not unmindful of the facts set out by my hon. friend, and I am not at all certain that this present time is the most propitious for bringing into effect these very considerable increases. Having regard to powers it will now have, I do not think anyone will consider it presumption on my part if I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) that in making appointments to the supreme court the first qualifications should be the highest integrity and ability, and also that no suggestion of political fitness as a major basis of appointment should be allowed to creep into appointments to that court.
I thank the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) for his obvious agreement with what I now say; for if we are to raise this court to the dignity and honour it must have in order to discharge its vast responsibilities, then above everything else ability, capacity and a sense of justice must characterize the appointments made to that bench.
In the United States-and I mentioned this on one other occasion-in order to guard the standard of their supreme court provision
was made for approval of appointments by the Senate. No doubt that system is inapplicable to our form of government, but it does ensure that appointments shall not be made that cannot pass the criticism and examination of that distinguished legislative body, which so often places the public good above private and political concepts. Unless in every appointment made to the Supreme Court of Canada qualifications transcend every political consideration, a blow will have been struck at the court from which it will not soon recover.
I believe the time has come to have only one court in this country known as a supreme court. It is most difficult for the laymen, if indeed it is not for the lawyer, to understand why in one province there is a supreme court while in another there is the court of king's bench. The time has come to amend the law so as to provide that there shall be one supreme court in Canada, so that when a judgment is given by the supreme court it will be generally known that it is the Supreme Court of Canada, and no other, to which reference is made.
The next point I make in connection with raising the standard of the bench-and I speak without any desire to arouse antagonism-is one which I suggest the minister might very well consider. Judges ought not to serve on royal commissions which have a political background. The inherent danger in the appointment of judges to royal commissions political in nature is that our judiciary is thereby undermined in the opinion of the people. I am not referring to royal commissions the purpose of which is to solve economic problems; I have in mind, for instance, the coal commission, which was presided over by the present hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll). I refer to royal commissions which have been appointed as a result of political criticism. It is my belief that the judiciary should not be called upon to serve on such commissions.
This matter was before the house in 1927. Mr. Bennett, who subsequently was president of the Canadian Bar Association, dealt with the matter from a nonpartisan standpoint. In 1927, when this act was before the house, he said, among other things:
Sometimes we have made appointments that have been political in their character. That is true; both sides have done it. It has been the reward sometimes for candidates who have run elections. Men have run elections, gone into a campaign, faced a constituency and said; Well, this is the only sure way by which I can get a judgeship. I know of cases like that, and so does my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and I regret to say that in every province in Canada you will probably find on the bench one or two men whose

appointments have been made solely because of the services they have rendered of a political character.
He went on to make this statement:
If you are to have justice administered efficiently and faithfully, if you are to have confidence in the judges of our courts, to rely upon their judgments and to feel that the differences between labour and capital and the great issues involving property and men's liberties, privileges and lives are honestly and justly dealt with, it can be done only by attracting to the bench men with the qualifications and attributes to which I have alluded.
That was in 1927. I remember well hearing the present Prime Minister, speaking before the Canadian Bar Association, express himself in sentiments very much the same. I think I speak for hon. members of the legal profession, as well as those outside of it, when I say that the people are asking that the appointments to the Supreme Court of Canada shall be such that the most benevolent political eye will not be able to discern qualifications based in part on political fitness.
We have set up a body that is to deal with the lives and the future of Canada, that will have the difficult task of settling major jurisdictional problems that arise between the dominion and the provinces. If this court is to discharge these vast responsibilities, above everything else it must be a court that merits and deserves, by reason of the fitness of those appointed to it, the custody of the future of the Canadian people. With all the power I can give to my words I ask the government that in making these appointments they select men who enjoy the respect of people everywhere in Canada, men whose honour and capacity is above reproach. If the government will do this, they will go far towards laying the foundation for the type of Supreme Court of Canada that the Canadian people wish to have.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill emphasizes the need of a legal committee of this house. Such a committee should have been set up long ago. I remember when my former leader appointed a committee to advise on and consider the revision of judges' salaries. At that time the government was having a great deal of difficulty in securing properly qualified men to fill vacancies in the high courts and other courts throughout the country. The committee recommended certain changes in the salaries and expenses of the judiciary.
This country has been well served by the large body of members of the bar who in the past have done so much for Canada in the matter of the administration of justice. Under the British North America Act the organization
Judges Act
of the courts is a provincial matter, but the dominion pays the salaries and retiring allowances.
This bill provides that the salary of the chief justice of the Supreme Court of Canada is to be increased from $20,000 to $25,000 and the salaries of the other judges from $16,000 to $20,000. The number of judges of the Ontario court of appeal has been increased by Ontario legislation from seven to nine. The judges who go out on circuit are doing good work, but they have to put up with considerable hardship in connection with hotel accommodation and other matters. Most of the hotels are constantly filled to capacity and these judges have great difficulty in securing suitable accommodation. I think the minister should make some allowance for this branch of the work.
The need of a legal committee has been demonstrated during this session. Three-quarters of the time of the house has been taken up in debating the principles of legal bills. We should not make a political football out of the administration of justice. This prevents the minister from filling vacancies and getting members of the bar to give up their private practices at great cost. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) represents that large body of men who are giving their time to this particular branch of work at great cost to themselves.	.
I am doubtful if the provision to increase the number of judges in the Ontario court of appeal from seven to nine is a wise provision. Ontario legislation has increased the number of judges of the high court from fourteen to sixteen. At one time the judges of the court of appeal had to reside in Toronto. It is difficult to obtain housing accommodation and at the present time one of them, owing to lack of housing accommodation, does not live in Toronto, even during court sittings.
We have a very able young supreme court judge who is now sitting in Ottawa, Mr. Justice G. A. Gale. He is a friend of the Speaker and of many other hon. members. He used to be in the firm of Mr. G. W. Mason, treasurer of the Law Society of Upper Canada, and is able to conduct cases in such a manner that his ability has received widespread recognition throughout the country. He is only one of a number of younger members of the bar who have taken up this work in Ontario at considerable cost to themselves.
Some arrangements should be made to provide allowances for these judges who travel on circuit. There are no houses available in Toronto, and like everybody else they are

Judges Act
forced to pay two or three times the ordinary value for a house. The increase in the number of judges of the high court of Ontario will provide some assistance for the judges who are now bearing the burden and the heat of the day on circuit throughout our province. Further assistance should be given in the way of travelling expenses. I do not see why the municipalities should have to pay all this when our judges are dealing with national work, and with 200,000 orders in council passed by this government.
I hope some arrangement will be made for consideration of this bill by a legal committee, because that is the only kind of body that can properly deal with it. Members of the bar, the judges and the attorneys general of the provinces could appear before that committee and give their views on these subjects, which are largely provincial. Under the British North America Act the organization of our courts is a provincial matter, and the dominion provides salaries and pensions for those who take up this most important work.

There is just one suggestion I should like to make. I do so partly because the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has suggested what I think would be a desirable change in terminology.
While I am on my feet, however, but without taking the time to repeat them, I want to support the views expressed so well by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). I feel it is not proper to increase both the salaries and the pensions of persons in these higher brackets when the government finds it so difficult to do the same thing for people in lower brackets. If this measure did only that, we would oppose it. We are in the position of having to accept the bill, because we recognize the need for an increased number of judges, but we shall shout "on division" as a protest against these increases in salaries already high.
The suggestion I should like to make as to terminology relates to the word "puisne". I suppose, like "Newfoundland", there are half a dozen pronunciations of it. I understand the correct pronunciation is "puny". It does not sound to me like a very complimentary title to give a judge. Certainly the salaries and pensions that go with being "puisne" are not puny. I wonder if consideration should not be given to changing that word to "associate". After all, that is what these justices of the supreme court are, other than the chief justice; they are associate
justices. I would hope that, when consideration is given to the suggestion of the hon. member for Lake Centre, consideration will be given also to the suggestion I have made.

May I point out to my hon. friend, however, that the naming of provincial courts is a provincial prerogative, and there is nothing that we in this House of Commons can do to change the name of the supreme court of Ontario except by making representations to the government and the legislature of that province. I would be quite in accord with doing so, but I think this is one of those dominion-provincial matters in connection with which it would have to be done tactfully. The hon. member also said that judges should not be appointed as members of royal commissions. Almost instantly we can see that there are certain disadvantages in the appointment of judges to royal commissions. Nevertheless upon further examination of the problem one can see great advantages in having them so act. After all, most royal commissions exercise judicial functions to a greater or lesser degree, and usually to a greater degree. The idea some people seem to have that the judicial function is something anyone with reasonable capacity can exercise without previous experience or training is a wrong one. Therefore when we have to look around in Canada for the most suitable members of royal commissions, judges are eminently fitted as candidates for such posts because of the fact they have been trained in exercising the function which is the chief function of a royal commission.

I think my hon. friend will agree with the observation I am now making, and perhaps will concur in my present agreement with the view he has expressed that in the face of the general problem the only thing a prudent and wise government can do is to balance the advantages against the disadvantages, and endeavour to secure the best of judicial talent for royal commissions, while at the same time not appointing judges to commissions which are likely to become the subject of political controversy.
As to the matter of salaries, I am greatly indebted to the hon. member for Lake Centre for the emphasis which he has placed upon the necessity of obtaining the very best talent that can be secured for the Supreme Court of Canada. I wonder whether we realize that, as a result of the supreme court amendment bill which we passed a few weeks ago, in a sense a new court is being established with greatly increased responsibilities and jurisdiction. The position of a final court of appeal is not only quite distinct and different from that of any other court in the country, but it is also quite different from the supreme court as it has been up until the present time, because it is now the court of last resort. The new court is to take the place of the privy council, which by general consent is one of the greatest appellate tribunals in history, and I suppose certainly the greatest appellate tribunal in the world today. We must remember that the function of deciding the law of our country in the last resort, which we are now turning over to the supreme court judges, was well described by the Earl of Carnarvon at the very time the Supreme Court of Canada was first set up. In doing so he used these words:
The supreme appellate authority of the empire or the realm is unquestionably one of the highest functions and duties of sovereignty. The power of construing, determining and enforcing" the law in the last resort is, in truth, a power which overrides all other powers since there is no act which may not in some form or other become the subject of a decision by the supreme appellate tribunal.
If we have any doubts as to the importance of the function which the court of last resort exercises in this or any other country, we only have to look back upon the effect which certain decisions of the privy council have had upon the constitution of our country. With respect to many judgments of the privy council, I venture to suggest that if any legislative body in Canada had attempted to achieve the same results by legislative action there would have been a tremendous outcry. So when we are setting up, as we have done, a court of last resort in Canada, it is not only preferable and advisable but imperative that we should secure the very best talent, men of the highest
Judges Act
integrity, because there can be few responsibilities in Canada the proper discharge of which will be more important to the welfare of our country than those of the chief justice and judges of the Supreme Court of Canada.
This being so, and having regard to the fact that all those likely to be suitable candidates for appointment to such a court are men in the high income brackets, while we have always expected them, and I think must continue to expect them, to make a substantial financial sacrifice by accepting appointment to this court, there is a certain salary to which we must reconcile ourselves if we are to induce mature lawyers of the highest ability to leave their home communities and come with their families to a new environment in order to serve upon the Supreme Court of Canada. It may be that the amount we are now providing is not enough; but whatever the figure may be that is considered enough, the fact that it is more than we pay some other official in Canada, or more than is earned by the general body of taxpayers in Canada, I suggest is irrelevant to the problem we are considering here.
Canada is not the only country that has to face this problem of offering salaries sufficient to induce lawyers of mature age to leave their home cities and their friends in order to serve upon a supreme court in a capital city. In the United States, for example, in spite of the egalitarian tendency in the matter of salaries, which is far stronger than in Canada, there is still a wide difference in this regard. In some departments there you may have a chief with twenty-five or thirty assistants, and there will be a difference of less than $50 between the salaries of the chief and his assistants, as in the interstate commerce commission, for one example. In that country, however, in spite of the egalitarian tendency to which I have referred, the associate judges of the supreme court in Washington are paid $25,000, whereas judges of the federal district courts of appeal, presumably men who after their appointment would usually remain in the communities in which they had been practising, receive $17,500, and the judges of the federal district trial courts are paid $15,000. So there is quite a wide spread.
If we are to secure the discharge in a proper manner of a function of government that has been described in the terms I previously quoted from the Earl of Carnarvon, we must not approach this matter in any penny-pinching spirit. For some time I acted as treasurer of a province, and I was not noted then as a spendthrift; but there are cases in which one can be penny wise and pound foolish, and I think this is eminently such a case. The total amount we propose to spend upon the

Judges Act
supreme court for the proper discharge of one of the most vital functions in our body politic is not in any sense exorbitant; it never has and never will be. The course we propose in this bill is wise, prudent and economical, a course for which we solicit the support of every hon. member of this house, regardless of party.
I should like to conclude with just a reference to the emphasis laid by the hon. member for Lake Centre-with which I am in entire agreement-on the suggestion that in appointments to this court political considerations should not be permitted to carry weight. In fairness to this government, however, I think I should draw to the attention of the hon. member the fact that within recent years there have been cases, which I think it would be invidious for me to identify by name, of appointment of judges who are now ornaments of the bench and who were appointed by this government in spite of the fact that they were of the opposite political persuasion-

speechtext:
In his concluding remarks the minister pointed out that the supreme court would have new duties resulting from the fact that it now becomes the final tribunal, not only in the ordinary civil cases that may come before it but also in the constitutional cases which in so many instances were previously decided by the privy council. I think it would be well for hon. members to
remember that the functions of that court have not yet been clearly defined so far as its constitutional responsibilities are concerned. For this reason I have some concern about the time at which this bill comes before us. The number of judges required to make that court an effective tribunal for all cases that may come before it, and the salaries necessary to attract the type of men who will give this judicial tribunal the very highest possible standing, to some extent relate to the new responsibilities that are to be accepted, and the extent to which these responsibilities will impose additional burdens upon the court. Hon. members of this committee do not yet know what is going to happen in regard to a large number of those constitutional cases which are called for decision by this court. In examining this bill and the arguments that have been put forward, it is necessary to remember that most of the constitutional appeals have related to matters of provincial concern. We do not yet know how those appeals are to be dealt with. That decision can be made only after consultation with the provinces. Undoubtedly it will be one of the first subjects discussed when the provincial governments meet the representatives of the dominion government on January 10. We do not yet know whether the provincial governments will ask for some other form of tribunal, or whether they will ask for some special procedure in relation to these cases.
While supporting without reservation the statement that it should be the desire of every one of us to raise the Supreme Court of Canada to a position of recognized preeminence in the judicial field, I have some concern about being called upon to express at this time an opinion as to the size of that court and the salaries that are required. It might have been advisable to defer the decision until after the meeting with the provinces, so that if agreement is reached, as we all hope it will be, the decision could be made with knowledge of the kind of procedure that is to be adopted in regard to the whole field of constitutional decisions.
I do not think, however, that there appears to be any question that this bill is to be adopted at the present time. I can therefore only reiterate what I have already said and what others have said: Let us hope, as Canadians, that the appointments which are made will give every Canadian reason to be proud of the Supreme Court of Canada. At the same time, in view of the observations I have made, I also urge that the representatives of the dominion government, when they meet the representatives of the provinces, bear in mind that the decisions then made will have

a continuing effect upon the status of the supreme court as our final court of resort in constitutional cases.
I have no thought of reviewing debates which have already taken place, but it will be remembered that one of our objections to a partial amendment to the constitution and a partial procedure for amendment of that constitution was related to this very fact. Some appeals can now go to the Supreme Court of Canada, and some-probably the largest number-can continue to go to the privy council, until there has been this joint decision. Let us hope, whatever procedure is followed as a result of the conference which opens on January 10, that we are not to have two types of constitutional appeal, but that our constitution will be one and indivisible.

speechtext:
I am always in order on these legal points, I am not opposed to increasing judges' salaries as such, but I am certainly not in accord with the reasons given by the Minister of Justice for doing so. He argues that in order to attract the best people to that particular field you have to pay them a high salary, and so forth, and so on. In going through life it has been my experience that you do not buy brains and judgment. You either have it or you have not. To justify the increases in salary on that argument is wrong, in my opinion. I have always found that the persons who have qualifications, ability and principles are generally those who are working for their living, because they believe in the principles they are working for, and they are not for sale. That has been my experience.
I want to leave this thought with the Minister of Justice. The taxpayers of Canada as a whole are the ones who will pay the
[The Chairman.]
salaries that we are setting now. Sitting here as an ordinary individual, who has no legal training, the thing that strikes me is that ninety-five per cent of the people who will pay the salaries will never be in a position to receive any of the super-justice dispensed by this particular body. They will never get before that court. Large corporations, provinces and others who are aggrieved and who have the necessary finances and can pay the fees required to employ legal talent, are the ones that this court will function for. On one occasion in the house I said-and I know there are over eighty lawyers in the house- that you can get as much justice as you can buy. Everyone raised the cry that that was a reflection on the judiciary. It is no such thing. I have never cast any aspersions on the judiciary. I made that statement, and it is a statement of fact. In order to get before this supreme court you will have to pay. I suggested to the previous minister of justice, Mr. Ilsley, that in looking over this whole legal set-up and the matter of dispensing justice, improvements should be made in the courts where ninety per cent of our people see justice dispensed, namely, in the magistrates' courts. These courts certainly do not give the average person in this country very much confidence in the way justice is meted out.
I am not opposed to getting the best men possible for these positions, but I do not agree with the idea that the best man possible for any position is the man who has his talents for sale, and sticks to that particular angle of it. People in certain positions should receive a large enough salary to get along on, and some in some positions require more than others.
During the Minister of Justice's tenure of office I should like him to give attention to the county courts, to which the ordinary citizen who is aggrieved and who has the finances may go. If he has the finances he is reasonably sure of getting some kind of balanced decision there. When the minister is looking at the question I wish he would take a look at the magistrates' courts. If he does I think he will agree that a large percentage of our young people who, because of lack of judgment in many instances, are thrown into penitentiaries for a year or two years, come out with a very bad picture in their minds as to the way in which justice is dispensed. Many of them carry on with that feeling. I suggest that the whole question of justice goes back to the courts of first instance. While it may be all right to get supermen for the super-court, it will not do the ordinary citizen of this country very much good unless he has the finances to get before it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.

I do not think I should let my hon. friend's observations pass unanswered. With the spirit of his reasoning I am in complete accord, but with great respect, I think that he has some of his premises wrong -some of his facts. For example, my hon. friend said that ninety per cent of the citizens of Canada could never get into this highest court of the land, and therefore they are in effect uninterested in the judgments which it renders. I suggest to my hon. friend that while many of this ninety per cent may not get into the highest court in the land as litigants, their lives are being affected every day by the interpretation which is placed by the highest court in the land upon, for example, a division of legislative powers between the dominion and the provinces.
One of the things we have to bear in mind is that it is not only by legislative action that the constitution of a country can be amended. When the fathers of confederation said that all the residuary powers in the country were to be exercised by the dominion, and the privy council in effect over a period of time interpreted property and civil rights within a province as being so wide as to include some residuary powers, they accomplished a change, and I think my hon. friend, being a practical and sensible man, would be the first to agree with me that any change of that kind, which is created by a court of last resort, goes to the hearthstone of every person in the country, no matter how humble he may be. This being so, the humblest man in Canada has a far greater interest in the composition of the Supreme Court of Canada than in some of the intervening appeal courts, because in the last resort it will be the Supreme Court of Canada which will interpret what the law of Canada shall be. The magistrates' courts and the high courts of the provinces, and the like, apply, in relation to the principle of stare decisis which we discussed at such great length on another occasion, the law as determined in the Supreme Court of Canada. With regard to the hon. member's observations as to magistrates' courts and the like, I am sure that upon reflection he will recall that they are all set up provincially, and that if any reforms are required in that direction his observations should be addressed to the provincial authorities.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SALARIES, TRAVELLING ALLOWANCES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I always like to hear the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He is the iconoclast of the house. He clears up these images so that they can be seen.
There is only one thing which I believe the minister missed. Up until the time of the amendment to the Supreme Court Act this
Judges Act
year a poor man could not get to the supreme court. He could go to the privy council in forma pauperis; in other words, he could apply to the courts for permission to go there, no matter how poor he might be. Provision was made this year, however, through an amendment introduced by my hon. friend, whereby anyone in this country, however humble, however poor, and despite his inability to meet the cost of litigation or the security for costs, may go to the Supreme Court of Canada, except so far as his constitutional freedoms are concerned, by simply making the necessary application. This was a step forward. My hon. friend asks where he would get counsel to argue the case. Well, no matter how eminent counsel may be, from my experience they will take anybody's case, regardless of fees, where a matter of injustice has been established. Today any person can go to the supreme court. Lack of finances does not now keep him back, and I am sure counsel could be found to take a case.

speechtext: I agree with everything the minister said, but he started off on the wrong foot by misquoting me.

speechtext: He said that I had said the average citizen is unaffected by and not interested in decisions of the supreme court. I did not say that, because I know he is. It was my intention merely to focus the attention of the Minister of Justice upon the fact that justice does not begin in the supreme court, it has its beginning in the courts of first instance. If you are lucky you will get justice; but I could mention many cases coming within my personal knowledge in which people had good cases but lacked the necessary financial backing to follow them up. I shall not say anything further on the point at the moment.

Mr. Chairman, this is the pertinent section of the bill. I should like to make some brief observations and ask one question.
I have received from the Pacific coast representations which indicate that the industry as a whole not only welcomes this bill but welcomes also the regulations which will be adopted thereunder. I am not suggesting for one moment that the government should turn over to the industry its power to make regulations. I am asking that, with a view to the drafting of workable and practicable regulations, consideration be given to both branches of the industry, so that we may have the assurance that the regulations will be based upon commercial standards and not solely upon laboratory, abstract and scientific principles. We want the assurance that they will be workable and devised for the protection of the industry as well as of the consuming public, either in this country or, as in this instance, the country to which the goods are exported.
I can assure the minister that under these circumstances he nfill find in all branches of

that are being harvested. In order to accomplish this he recommends, amongst other things:
1.	Fire protection must be greatly increased.
2.	The rate of planting denuded areas of productive forest land must be greatly increased.
3.	Logging methods must be regulated to prevent destructive exploitation, and to ensure full regeneration of cut-over lands.
4.	New systems of tenure and taxation need to be formulated to encourage private forestry and to remove causes compelling liquidation.
5.	There must be a more intensified research in the practice of silvicultural methods.
6.	Facilities and funds must be provided for extensive forestry research.
This is a responsibility that faces every province. It is a program which entails heavy expense, but an expense that is small in relation to the revenue derived from our forest industries. It could be said that, as our natural resources belong to the provinces, they should be responsible for their protection, but this overlooks the fact that the dominion, quite apart from all other benefits, derives considerable revenue from our forest industries and the subsidiary industries that they sustain. We undoubtedly have an obligation to assist the provinces, and to do so in a way that will contribute most to the common good.
During the course of the debate in committee when we were discussing the resolution preceding the bill, many statements were made which demonstrated the interest of members in the subject of forestry, but in some cases they also indicated that some members do not altogether realize the extent of the work at present being carried on in our forestry division. For example, one member stated that my department "had no experience really in regard to forests", and suggested that we should consult the provinces, overlooking the fact that until 1930 the dominion had direct control over 33,000 square miles of national forests. While in 1930 the government handed over our natural resources in the west, including our national forests, to the four western provinces, we by no means eliminated our dominion forest service. It continued to operate very efficiently, in spite of the limited appropriations that were available, and through close and continued co-operation with the provinces has been able to provide most useful services.
By maintaining three forest products laboratories and five forest experimental stations, much valuable information has been secured. If any of the members wish to visit

our forest products laboratory in Ottawa, I am sure that they will find it just as interesting as I did when I visited it for the first time.
Through district offices established across Canada, close contact is maintained with the provincial authorities. In addition, during the summer months thirty-one forest survey parties have been in the field compiling information on such subjects as forest inventories, fire danger research, regeneration, and the growth and yield in various forest regions. Many of these parties have been working in provincial areas securing data which is available to both the provinces and the dominion. By means of air photography, and by using new techniques developed in the department, considerable information has been secured as to forest resources.
1 think hon. members will agree that all this is good as far as it goes, but I do not think anyone believes that it is sufficient to provide adequate protection for the forest resources of Canada. I mentioned a few moments ago the limited appropriations, which were reduced from $1,427,000 in 1930-31 to a low of $241,000 in 1934-35. Since then our appropriations for forest services have been gradually increased until we have in the estimates today the sum of $1,418,000 for 1949-50, and additional sums provided for special projects amounting to nearly two and one-half million dollars.
It was in 1943 that eight of the provinces submitted a brief outlining recommendations for a forestry program, some of which have already been partly implemented. The provinces recommended first that the dominion government grant assistance to the provinces for forest protection, including protection against fire, insects and diseases; second, that the dominion government consider the advisability of intensifying research on forest problems; and third, that the dominion government give special consideration to the whole question of conservation and proper utilization and management of forest resources as a permanent national forest policy.
I have said that some of these recommendations have already been partly implemented. The forest insect control board was set up in 1945, consisting of representatives from the forestry branch, the Department of Agriculture, and the provinces, and appropriations for forest entomology were increased from $70,000 a year to $1,087,000. At the present time this board reports to the Department of Mines and Resources, while the research work in forest entomology is undertaken by the Department of Agriculture. A forest entomological laboratory at Sault Ste. Marie was built by the province of Ontario, and in

1945 was equipped and staffed by the dominion government. A new forest pathological laboratory is also being completed at the Sault with dominion funds, and is being staffed by the dominion. This will be, I may say, one of the most up-to-date laboratories of its kind in the world.
Our forest products laboratories carry out research to promote the more efficient use of our forest resources, to prevent waste, and to provide new uses for species of wood now used only to a limited extent.
Fire of course provides the great hazard that annually destroys millions of dollars' worth of timber, and this is a danger that must be faced by the dominion and the provinces together. I think hon. members will be interested in the statistics for 1948, which show that 23 per cent of all fires were started by smokers, 18 per cent by lightning, 17 per cent by camp fires, 12 per cent by railways, 11 per cent by settlers; and 19 per cent were attributable to various other causes. In the same year, 1948, there were 5,368 forest fires in the provinces, and the total damage, including fire-fighting costs, is estimated at more than $8,500,000.

It does seem to me that everything possible should be done to impress upon the minds of our people the immense importance of protection of the forests. There is not only the damage to the soil which results from excessive cutting or the burning over of areas which are not replanted; there is also the loss of water power and the very great danger that fire or excessive cutting may result in communities which have been built up around the production of forest products being left without the raw materials necessary for that purpose. subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
Before section 1 is carried, Mr. Chairman, I should like to state to the minister my views on the substance of subclause (a) and ask for his opinion on what is proposed in that clause. The minister was unable to attend the meetings of the committee on agriculture, and for that reason there was no one there to give an explanation of government policy.
The amendment to the act reduces from a block of nine sections to a block of six that area which may be removed from a township that is eligible for prairie farm assistance. It reduces the average yield in the block which may be removed from something over fourteen bushels to anything over ten. My point is that within this six-section rectangular block, when it is removed, there may be one or two farmers with a crop of less than eight bushels per acre and therefore a crop failure according to the provisions of this act. I do not believe that any farmer within an eligible township, and who has a crop of less than eight bushels per acre, should be removed from the provisions of this act. I think it is discriminatory to remove any farmer on that basis.
I want to point out that in the committee we tried to have this section amended so that no farmer within a six-section block should be taken out of an eligible township if his yield was under eight bushels per acre. I would point out that in 1947, while there were 2,644 townships eligible under the act, only 17 part townships were removed. I might further point out that the departmental official, Mr. Matte, gave us some interesting

information when he said that the board of review went over the experience they have had with 300 townships. He found that there were just three instances in which a block of six sections would have been removed. In these three instances there was just one farmer with a yield of less than eight bushels per acre. If this provision could be changed so that no farmer would be excluded from getting the bonus if he had a yield of less than eight bushels per acre it would certainly cost the government very little money, perhaps just a few hundred dollars. As. the departmental official, Mr. Matte, said, in the 300 townships only one farmer was excluded. Therefore if this provision was changed to that extent it would cost the government only two or three hundred dollars to give a bonus to a farmer who has in fact a crop failure.
I know the minister has done a great deal toward improving this act, and I think it would be a small change and I should like to have his views on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, although I was not able to be present in the agriculture and colonization committee I did read all of the evidence that was taken there, and therefore I am well aware of the views which the hon. member for Assiniboia holds. The opinion which is held is one which I have been trying to remove from the minds of persons in western Canada generally ever since the act was enacted in 1939. We do not make payments to anyone because of the small or large amount of wheat that he may produce on an acre of land. That is not done. And to put up the argument at any time that, because a man has only eight bushels of wheat to the acre, he ought to have payment is not in accordance with any part of the principle of this act. The act simply says that we use the yield of wheat on the land in a township for the purpose of finding out whether it has been dry or not. We do not make payment on the basis of wheat. A man does not have to grow any wheat in order to get payment. A man does not have to grow any grain at all in order to get payment. A man may have nothing but grass with livestock running on it and he will still get payment. Payments are not made on the basis of wheat at all. We take the yield of wheat only to find out how dry it has been in a certain area. And when we find that it has been so dry that the average yield of wheat in a township is eight bushels or less, to the acre, when wheat is at the present price, we say that payment ought to be made to every farmer in that township.
Prairie Farm Assistance Act
In so far as this particular section is concerned, as I said before, when the average yield was more than fourteen bushels to the acre then nine or more sections of land in a rectangular form might be removed from the benefits of the act. It was found by experience, and from the criticisms of the municipal associations, that we had not given sufficient thought to the matter when we put in nine, whatever the figure should have been, because there is no way you can get a rectangular block of nine sections unless it be three by three. Therefore that was not a very good figure to have taken.
In this particular amendment we say six instead of nine. And when it is six it is one strip up one side of a township, or it may be two by three running directly away from the ineligible area, or it may be two by three running up and down alongside the area. There are quite a number of ways in which you can figure six townships and still get it rectangular, as against a number that you can figure out with nine. Then, of course, the condition with regard to the greater numbers is much the same. It could be twelve; it could be some other figure and still be rectangular. But the reason for changing from fourteen to ten is that the act as it stood was operative up to twelve bushels to the acre until wheat rose in price from down around 50 or 60 cents up to over 80 cents. There is one section of the act that is not operative at all and has not been operative since wheat passed 80 cents a bushel some years ago. That part is the section which provides for payments between eight and twelve bushels. Payments are made there only when the price of wheat is under 81 cents. When it is over 80 cents it cuts out altogether. That again is just a means of figuring out what the returns are that a farmer is likely to get in an area. While that was operative we said fourteen bushels to the acre was the point at which you started to take land out of an eligible township. We have been operating with the section in during the last few years, and there was no way of taking land out until it got up to that particular level, with the result that many sections of land were permitted to remain in where the yield was not below eight bushels to the acre on the average. Therefore, criticisms were made that some people, who had very high yields not only of wheat but of oats and barley or very good grass crops, were getting paid at a time when some other people were not being paid. We have simply reduced it down to having the same relationship to eight now as it had to twelve before. It is ten now before you start to take it out as against eight when it comes in. It was fourteen before as against twelve;

Prairie Farm Assistance Act so that unless we get down to the point where we are getting 80 cents a bushel for our wheat there will be no reason for having to figure any change.
The only other thing I should like to say about the matter is that I think the argument that was put up by hon. members of the committee against the proposed amendment of the member for Assiniboia, and which resulted in its being voted down when it was before the committee, is a sound argument, namely, that not only are you starting to make payments on the yield of wheat that an individual has, but you are trying to base this legislation more or less on an individual basis. I know that in the committee hon. members from other parts of Canada were desirous of knowing what is a section. It is about 640 acres of land. What is the size of a farm in western Canada? I think the impression was given that a section of land is about the size of a farm. That of course is not correct. In western Canada the average-size farm is more nearly a half-section of land than a section. As a matter of fact it is under three hundred acres. A short time ago I had occasion to look at our own figures to find out how many farms there are in Saskatchewan that have two sections or more of land. It is less than two per cent. In other words, this idea that farms in western Canada are big carries us away sometimes. On the average they are not as big as some people think they are. The average farm is much smaller than was suggested the other day. While you would not be getting down to an individual basis if you made it a section of land, yet you would be getting down to a unit so small that it would not meet the purposes that are fundamental in the act itself. One of these purposes is that a man should not be encouraged to stay on land that is never going to produce a good crop at any time. In order to emphasize what that means I shall give the committee a few facts with regard to the area where the payments have been highest.
Take a block of land in the southwestern part of Saskatchewan, with its west boundary on the boundary of Alberta and its east boundary, No. 4 highway, running north from the United States border through Swift Current, crossing the Saskatchewan river at Saskatchewan Landing, directly north of Swift Current; and take as the north boundary the South Saskatchewan river, and the south boundary the United States border- in that area there are 369 townships. In that area there are only three townships which have received payment in only one year out of the last nine years. In that area there are only four townships which have received payment for only two years, and

only one that has received payment for only three years. Then, there are 14 that have received payment for four years, and 31 that have received payment for five years out of nine. That is just slightly more than half the period. There are only 69 townships in that block of 369 that have not had payments for more than five years. In other words 300 townships in there have had payments five years or more.

speechtext: That is in Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
Yes, in Saskatchewan-in that one block in Saskatchewan. Those who prepared the act had in mind two things, one of which was to assist the people in remaining on areas where it is very difficult for them to remain until such time as we can work out some plan to have them resettled. The other was to determine, by getting information just as we are getting it today, what areas ought to be resettled.
I believe there will be very little doubt in the minds of most people that when an area has had payments for five years out of nine- and 31 of these townships received them five years out of nine, 82 received them six years out of nine, 114 received them seven years out of nine, 75 received them eight years out of nine, and 29 received them nine years out of nine,-there is no doubt that someone should begin to arrange some plan to have them resettled rather than continue paying to keep them on.
Therefore I say it is not desirable to have a section put into the bill which says that if a man is living on a piece of land with a yield of less than eight bushels to the acre he ought to be paid, no matter what his neighbours are getting off their lands. He may be living on a sandhill. It may be that he is not utilizing his land to the best advantage, as some of his neighbours are. There may be many reasons. But we are not paying on the basis of what he produces in wheat; we are paying on the basis of what it is possible for him to do because of the climatic conditions in the whole area in which he lives. We desire to have the act maintained on that basis, rather than to have it put on an individual basis in the sense that some people will be paid, while others are not, on a basis different from that on which others are being paid.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
I agree that the attitude of the government has always been that this act should not be placed on an individual basis. I also differ from the minister in his belief that it should not be placed on an individual basis. I do agree that something has to be done, and very soon, to take care of people farming in the area the minister has just mentioned.

I do not want to go outside the act in the discussion but if the government is interested in doing something to remove people from the provisions of the act, so that they will not have crop failures year in and year out, then of course it should do something about irrigation. However I am not suggesting at this time that the purposes of the act be changed.
The act applies only when there is a township with a crop failure and, if there is a township with a crop failure, then it can be applied to half townships with crop failures and thus, on a basis of rough justice, to people in a township or a half township. All I asked under paragraph (a) was that the minister should see that one or two farmers who are discriminated against at the present time should be allowed to get payments.
While I am on my feet I should like to deal with paragraph (b) of section 1, which deals with bringing into an eligible township a block of land outside the eligible township and lying within an ineligible township. This provision used to be applied to a rectangular block of nine sections, and has now been reduced to a rectangular block of six sections.
I point out to the minister that when he takes in a rectangular block he is very likely taking in some farmers who have more than eight bushels to the acre and, beyond question, he is leaving out many farmers in the ineligible neighbouring township who have a yield of less than eight bushels of wheat to the acre. I do not wish to leave the impression that I do not know a farmer can be paid for a crop failure, even though he does not grow wheat. Wheat is taken only as a yardstick by which payments are made.
In the committee I suggested that the clause be changed, and that instead of adding to an eligible township rectangular blocks of a given size the government should add to the township a section or string of sections contiguous to the eligible township, so long as the yield in those sections was less than eight bushels to the acre.
The minister added strength to my argument when he pointed out that there are more half-section farms in western Canada than farms of any other size. My suggestion was that after an area has been declared eligible the department should go on from there and add on sections of land-not individual farms-but sections of land in which the yield of wheat was less than eight bushels to the acre.
Irrespective of the government's attitude or the purposes of the act as set out by the minister, I say without fear of successful contradiction that the farmers of western Canada are interested in having the payments made on an individual basis. They
Prairie Farm Assistance Act are interested, particularly after a township has been declared eligible, that the individual sections of land outside the township may be included.
With that in mind, in the committee on agriculture I offered an amendment. The chairman of the committee said that the committee did not have the right to change the bill, but that after it was passed in committee we might tag on to it certain recommendations to the government. Therefore my suggestion would not even have changed the bill, but would have merely brought to the attention of the minister the majority opinion of the committee on agriculture, had that recommendation been accepted. My amendment was that the committee recommend that the government consider the advisability of amending Bill No. 185 by deleting subparagraph (b) of the proposed new section 7, in section 1 of the bill, and substituting therefor the following:
(b) Where a section of land lies within an ineligible township and has a side that lies alongside an eligible township or is a section which lies alongside an eligible section or a corner of which touches the corner of an eligible township or an eligible section, such section of land1 shall be eligible for award as though it were a complete township.
If that recommendation had been made to the government and if the government had changed the bill accordingly it would mean that farmers alongside an eligible township who had a crop failure because of drought could become eligible under the act. The yeas were Argue, Bryce, Fair, Wright. The nays were Bennett, Blue, Corry, Darroch, Dumas, Elderkin, George, Hetland, Jutras, Kent, Laing, Leger, MacKenzie, McCubbin, Murray (Oxford), Richard (St. Maurice-Lafleche), Roberge, Studer.
I would like to point out that the Conservatives on that committee were not responsible for the defeat of my amendment. I do not think there were any Conservative members from western Canada present when the vote was taken. The Conservative members from eastern Canada apparently felt that they did not have sufficient information to judge whether my suggestion was a good one or not. There were four yeas and eighteen nays, and among those eighteen nays was the hon. member for Maple Creek and the hon. member for Humboldt. How members of the agriculture committee who came from Saskatchewan could vote against a suggestion that a recommendation be made to the government to improve the Prairie Farm Assistance Act is entirely beyond me.
I could not understand the vote of the hon. member for Maple Creek because a large part of these payments have been made in his

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
constituency. I know it is said that the rural municipal association wanted this amendment and I think it can be said that they thought it would be a step in the right direction. I venture to say that there are not a dozen farmers in the dried-out areas of Saskatchewan who would vote against the suggestion I made in the committee.
Here is what the hon. member for Humboldt said in the committee, and I quote from page 11:
Mr. Chairman, I do not think we should change it very much; as a matter of fact, I do not think we should change it at all. This is a thing that we have been asking for over the years, and now that we have it here in the form in which it is before us, X think we should accept it.
As I have said before and as I say now, the present act does not go far enough. I am sorry the Liberal members of that committee did not support my amendment. If it had passed it would not have defeated the government, it would not even have criticized the government; it was merely asking the government to consider whether or not the act could be broadened to include farmers who have a crop failure. Irrespective of whether the minister is satisfied with this act, I am not, and I shall raise this matter at every session of parliament.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member who has just taken his seat has referred to the agriculture committee and lest there be any misunderstanding in that connection may I say that I attended in that committee during the forenoon and expressed myself with regard to his suggestion. I believed that it was something that I could support and that it should be sent on as a recommendation. However, I was not present when the vote was taken. The debate on the combines matter was going on in the house and I felt that I had some responsibility in that connection and could not be present when the vote in the committee was taken.
Having said that, there are one or two matters I should like to ask the minister about. I think the amendment does meet a situation about which there has been criticism over the years. Personally I have felt that some change along this line should be made and that as far as possible the aim should be to have the payments made on an individual basis.
At all times I have endeavoured to be fair and have said that I thought it would be impossible to make these payments on an individual basis without a substantial increase in the amounts presently deducted from the producers. In order to be in position to bring to the attention of the committee certain suggestions in connection with the Prairie Farm

Assistance Act amendments, and to keep this matter non-political, I wrote to various municipalities in my constituency.
In the southern part of my constituency there are large areas which have had continuing drought such as was referred to a moment ago by the Minister of Agriculture. I pass on from there to a matter on which I have received correspondence as late as today. I should like the minister to answer a question that I will propound to him based on what is now taking place in the province of Saskatchewan. A series of mass meetings are being held during the present week, beginning on the 28th of November at Hodge-ville and continuing in various parts of the province, regarding payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. They are extensively advertised. The areas in the southern part of the province are those to which the minister made reference a moment ago when he gave statistics of certain townships that for a period of seven successive years had received payments under this act.
As I said a moment ago, these meetings have been extensively advertised in the press, and are given widespread publicity in the Western Producer. The situation in many of these areas of central and southern Saskatchewan is more serious than it has been since the days of the thirties when drought swept everything away except hope and determination on the part of those living there. These farmers are meeting together for the purpose of having some provision made by parliament for a temporary increase in benefits for this year under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. Several farmers in different areas have written to me, apparently without collaboration, intimating that the government has 45781-158
Prairie Farm Assistance Act under consideration the raising of benefits for this year under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act by $1 an acre under legislation to be introduced before the end of this session or at the next session of parliament. That is one of the matters coming before these meetings. Apparently those responsible for organizing them are doing so in a widespread area. The second thing they are asking is whether or not, having regard to the failures they have suffered, consideration is being given either under this act or outside it-I presume it would be within the purview of this act-to the supplying of farmers in these areas with seed wheat at reduced prices in order to enable them to carry on and face the next year with at least the opportunity of again challenging nature, as they do in these areas, by seeding crops in the springtime.
I know in my own constituency registered seed grain is being offered by municipalities at $2.40 a bushel. Prices are very high for seed barley. The farmers in these municipalities are asking whether or not, having regard to the fact that in these areas there is an emergency condition so great in scope as to merit national attention, the government has in mind the granting of either of the requests to which I have made reference. These are matters that transcend any consideration of party, or the location in the house which any hon. member occupies for the moment. They are matters which affect all members from Saskatchewan. As I see it, being a question of national moment inasmuch as the drought areas affect a population of 150,000 or 200,000 people, these are matters about which I am sure the people living in these areas would like to have some assurance from the Minister of Agriculture as to what is going to be done.

Generally speaking, as I said on second reading, I think the P.F.A.A. is a good act. I think these amendments are going to improve it. On the other hand they do not remove some of the main criticisms we hear against it. I want to deal with the first two amendments contained in this bill. First is the amendment to section 7(a). Would the minister say the real purpose of this amendment is to deny the bonus to a farmer who has suffered crop failure within an eligible township? I think he will agree that is not the purpose, but that the purpose is to deny the bonus to a farmer in an eligible township who has over ten bushels to the acre.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS

speechtext:
Nevertheless the yield in those six sections must be over ten bushels to the acre. As I pointed out on second reading, under this section farmers residing in an eligible township with a total crop failure have been denied the bonus, not because they were residing in a district where the yield was good but simply because they happened to be adjacent to a small block that had a good yield. Surely the minister must agree that a farmer residing in a township where 28 sections of land, we will say, have had a total crop failure should be considered as residing in an area where there has been a large degree of crop failure, and therefore should be entitled to the bonus. In that case the minister could not suggest that we are asking for the bonus for a farmer just because he happens to have a poor piece of land. That is the general condition. The yield on the six or nine sections is not to be taken as indicating the general condition in that township. If a farmer suffering a crop failure happens to be unfortunate enough to reside on one quarter of that six-section area, I should say he would be far more entitled to the bonus than the farmer who happened to have his farm adjacent to a small block of land where there was a crop failure.
I give the minister this example, which happened in the Rumsey area. A township had been declared eligible; then in one corner they found six sections with a yield of around twenty bushels to the acre. They could not take out those six sections because the minimum number was nine. So they added three sections that had practically a total crop failure, but still the average was above fourteen bushels. The minister must admit that it was hardly fair to include the other three sections. I took up the matter with the P.F.A. officials here, who said it was very unfortunate but that as the act was worded they had no alternative. Therefore I suggest that under this amendment those officials should be given power to use their discretion in determining whether or not certain sections should be denied the benefits of the act.
I noticed that in committee the assistant director under P.F.A.A. said this very seldom happened. Well, it seems to me that whenever it has happened it has been in my constituency, because several such cases have been drawn to my attention. I took up two of them with the officials here at Ottawa, but when I found I could not get anywhere I did
247f

not bring any more up. However, I know of several instances in my constituency where this has happened, and I imagine it has happened elsewhere as well.
When this bill was being considered in committee the hon. member for Battle River moved this amendment:
Notwithstanding anything contained in this section, no section of land having an average of less than eight bushels to the acre shall be denied the bonus in an eligible township.
That amendment was ruled out of order, and later was voted down as a recommendation; yet I am satisfied that a majority of the Liberal members from western Canada were in favour of it. I had been discussing it with them in the lobby and found that they approved it; but they found themselves, I suppose, in the unfortunate position of having to agree with the ruling of the government. How could anyone from western Canada disagree with that amendment? It is based upon a sound principle; it is fair, as I am sure the minister himself would be the first to agree. It would not provide for the payment of a bonus to a man just because he happened to have a piece of sandy land. It would provide the bonus to a farmer because a majority of the land in the township was in the same fix as his piece of land. It seems to me very unfair to deny the bonus just because a man happens to be adjacent to five other sections that have a high yield. Surely the fact that he is adjacent to thirty-one sections of land that had a crop failure should be a better argument for giving him the bonus; and on that basis it defeats the very argument made by the minister.
With respect to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Assiniboia, in committee, had I been there I would have supported it because it was an attempt to get away from that rectangle which the minister seems to love so much.
