speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
I think the last point brought up by the hon. member should be dealt with, because when this bill was drafted a year ago it contained a provision which would have met the requests that have been made by the hon. member for Assiniboia and the hon. member for Acadia. The meeting held in Regina a year ago last June, which was referred to in committee when this bill was under consideration, was attended by representatives of the three prairie provinces, and also by representatives of the municipal associations of those provinces. At that meeting these two amendments which are before the house were discussed, and also a third amendment. The third amendment was based upon the idea that the federal government is not the only government that is responsible for giving assistance to people who are in difficulties. The argument put forward was the argument that has so often been put forward in the house, namely, that when the responsibility was all on the province and Ottawa did not acknowledge any responsibility for the situations-and they did not down until a recent date-we did at one time say that until twenty-five municipalities were in difficulty in a province we would not take any responsibility. When twenty-five municipalities were in difficulty we considered that the problem was too big for the provincial governments, and then we would consider doing something about it. That was in the days before I came to Ottawa; but having been in the government of one of the provinces that suffered most, I know fairly well what was the position that was taken.
Then when it came to a matter of removing responsibility, we said right down until about the middle of the thirties that as soon

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
as it got down to the point where there were ten municipalities-not ten townships but ten municipalities, each of them having nine townships in it which need assistance-then the dominion government had nothing more to do with it and the provincial government and the municipalities had to take care of the whole problem. That was the practice prior to 1939. Then in 1939 we brought in this bill. At the time the bill was brought in we submitted the question to the provinces as to whether they desired to co-operate with us and pay some money into the fund, just as the federal government was paying money into the fund, in order to take care of all the persons that might be in difficulties in the area. All I can say at the moment is that in spite of the fact that it was not in all cases the same governments that are there now, the governments that were there then were not satisfied to enter into the plan on that basis. So what we did was to bring in this bill, and what we said in the house when we put it through was that we were going to ask the people of all Canada to help in making assistance payments in the full townships, and that the remainder of the area should be left to the provinces and the municipalities to take care of, as we thought that the district would be small enough then for them to take care of it.
Everyone here knows the history of it. The municipalities and the provinces did just what they nearly always do. They say: When once the dominion government get into a field of this kind they will eventually be forced to do it all, so we will just let them do it. I presume that is the attitude that has been taken, because I have met them many times and discussed the question with them. The last time we discussed it was a year ago last June at this meeting in Regina that I referred to. At that meeting the representatives of the provinces agreed that we should put in this act an amendment which would state, in effect, that the dominion government would be prepared to accept from each of the provinces a payment which would be proportionate to the amount of land that they were asking to have taken care of as against the amount of land that we were taking care of; and that if that were done, then they would recommend to us the taking in of these areas round about the areas eligible for payment, and having recommended that they be taken in, they would pay in their proportionate amount which, as has been stated by some of the members, would be small.
It has been argued that the amount the federal government would have to put in, in order to take care of these extras, is small

as compared with the amount that we are now putting in. What we argued was that the amounts the provinces would put in under these circumstances would be very small as compared with the amount that we ourselves would be putting in. Then it was understood that this recommendation would be taken back to the governments of the three provinces and that they in due course would inform me as to whether or not they desired to have that amendment and whether or not they were prepared to carry on under it.
As I stated a moment ago, a bill with that provision in it was drafted a year ago; and since a year ago I have had letters from all three of the provinces saying that they were not prepared to recommend it or to carry on under it. That is the only reason it is not in here now. It could have been brought in and it would have been brought in for the purpose of making it possible to take care of the very areas that are being talked about. Some have said: Why not make it an L? If you make it an L, you will still have a township in the corner of the L, and in all probability everybody will come along and say it should be taken care of. It does not make any difference what form, shape or number you put in, there will always be that road allowance where the crop will be just about as bad on the other side as it is on this side. Our hope was to settle that question so that we would not have to explain to all the other people in Canada who are helping to pay for this assistance that they are not paying for it all, but that the province is also putting a certain amount of money in; and I still hold that is the only solution for the problem that is continuously put up by the hon. member for Acadia and by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I would suggest to both of them that they have much greater influence than I have with the governments back home. If they can just persuade those governments to allow the other amendment, which would have been the third amendment on this occasion if they had not objected to it, if they would just agree to that other amendment-and we do not think it would cost them a great deal-we will get rid of all those political speeches such as the one we heard a few moments ago.
I do not know that it is proper to take a division of opinion in a committee such as the one to which this bill was referred, bring it up here and say this member voted that way, the other member voted the other way, I voted so and so, and base an argument on that. Either it is right to do the thing that was suggested or it is wrong to do it. I think we are all prepared to argue this matter out

in the country in the same way as we argue it in the committee or as we argue it in the house. I do not know what other members have found but as for myself-and I naturally come in contact with this argument more than anyone else-I have never yet met with a group of farmers, either behind closed doors, or out in the open, who have not agreed, after the argument was all over, that the position I am taking now in this committee is the correct one and the one that I should continue to take, so as not to put before the house propositions which might be opposed by other parts of Canada because they are not reasonable. I think that these provinces should be prepared to come forward with a certain amount of money and put it into the treasury-and it would be small-and justify the position that other people are taking all over Canada. If they did so they would be making it possible to deal with the small blocks without compelling other parts of Canada to bear the entire burden.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act

speechtext:
The other question
referred to assistance in procuring seed grain.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
It involves the same principle. This government has never intentionally provided seed grain to any of the western provinces or to any other province. We have had applications since I have been in the Department of Agriculture from I think every province in Canada for assistance in connection with the provision of seed, and we have always taken the position that that is a provincial responsibility. It is true that back in the thirties we assisted the provinces in getting lines of credit so that they could provide the seed, but the seed has always been provided by the provinces. We did get into some controversy when the credit was not being met by some provinces as to whether we should pay, and in some instances we probably did have to pay, but it was not intentional. There was no intentional action taken at any time by this government to provide seed. The action has always been taken by the provinces. We take the position that the direct relationship is farmer to municipality and municipality to the province. In connection with seed, up to now we have never gone by that in any of the provinces of Canada.
The other matter of providing assistance in other directions is looked at in this way. We have taken the position that the assistance which we give under prairie farm assistance is our share. This year it runs to some $17 million. The provinces have set up a plan to take care of providing seed, feed and other supplies to farmers. They tell me that they are paying, I think, half of the amount of the freight to those who are making demands in other directions. The provinces have said it is impossible to give assistance to the full amount that is being asked. We have replied that we think we are paying our share through P.F.A.A. Therefore I doubt very much whether when they are all through the provinces will have paid $17 million out in the undertaking. When they are all through they will still be quite short of paying out $17 million. In Saskatchewan about $3, and in Alberta it would probably be about $2, will be put up by the federal government for every $1 that is put up by the farmer. Therefore we think that of this amount we shall pay $3 for every $1 that the farmer puts up. For that reason we shall probably be putting up about two-thirds of the $17 million. I doubt very much whether the provinces will get anywhere near that amount in the assistance that they are giving. We are simply suggesting that there is a possibility of their giving more assistance, and they have not denied it at any time.

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
They discussed the question with us. We have turned it back to them with the suggestion that if they think any more is required the provinces ought to be able to pay it in view of the fact that the fund is putting up this $17 million. And that is the way the discussion has ended.

speechtext:
The minister referred to various meetings with farmers in the province in which he found the farmers in general agreement with him on this subject. I was going to suggest that perhaps his stand on this matter was not as definite at some of these meetings as it is in the house where he has responsibility. However, I did not rise to speak politically. I merely rose to back up the argument of my colleague, the hon. member for Assiniboia, who has said the things that I myself would have said if I had been as well qualified to say them, because this particular hon. member has an intimate knowledge of the subject. It is fitting, too, that I should follow, at least for a moment, the path of the hon. member for Lake Centre, because geographically I start where he leaves off. His constituency and mine join at the town of Hanley, which this year is in the middle of an area which is affected by the various disadvantages which have affected farmers this year.
I should like to back up the plea of these hon. members. From that point which I have mentioned the township line runs east and west. From Hanley we go straight up my constituency towards Saskatoon city through a part of the farm land which is so very seriously affected this year. It has been just one thing after another. No doubt the minister knows about the early frost in June which cut the wheat completely down to the ground. That might have been all right if it had been followed by rain which would have caused stooling out.
As the minister well knows, the crop in 1915 was one of the best crops we have had in the province of Saskatchewan. Unfortunately, this year, while it started out somewhat similarly, it did not follow the path that the weather followed in 1915. The rain did not come in the same quantities and so we had the condition that now obtains.
The next particular thing was the grasshopper. I remember driving from my town to the town of Dundurn once this summer and stopping in the car to let some of my family who were in it watch these grasshoppers cross the road by the million. I looked over the stations in both Dundurn and Hanley where the farmers were working night and day mixing the grasshopper poison and scattering it about the fields.

The districts up along the Beaver creek where the land is sandy are a particular problem. Whether or not people should make an attempt to farm that land is not my particular business here, but my plea is for some assistance to the people who are trying to eke out a living in that particular part of the country. This year these people will be almost wholly dependent upon the grants which they receive of $2.50 an acre if their yield is below four bushels of wheat to the acre and $1.50 per acre if the crops are from four to eight bushels.
I should like to join with my colleague who pleaded for more generous assistance, both in regard to the amount of money paid and in regard to bringing this grant to a more nearly individual basis.
I should like to draw the minister's attention to something that might solve part of this problem for that particular part of the country, namely, co-operative irrigation schemes which are being tried there, and which I think should have assistance both from the federal government and from the provincial government. I refer to projects where water is being pumped out of a branch of the south Saskatchewan river onto this flat land adjacent to the country east of Dundurn. I think that irrigation project could form a good testing ground for the later and larger irrigation scheme to which we have so long looked forward.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
It is not my intention to take up many minutes of the time of the committee because what I wanted to say has been very well said by the hon. member for Acadia. I want to endorse his remarks wholeheartedly. A statement was made by the Minister of Agriculture on which I should like to get some more information, namely, the amendment that has been discussed by the provinces with him, and which he says they have recently refused to agree to. If the minister has a copy of that amendment perhaps he could read it to us and also tell us who have refused to agree with it. I feel that the request which I made to the committee the other day, and also the request which was made by the hon. member for Assiniboia, are reasonable and would relieve much of the dissatisfaction that exists at the present time.
On many occasions the minister has agreed to amendments being made to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act since it was first introduced in 1939. To a very large extent these amendments have done away with dissatisfaction with the act. There is one matter that has not been mentioned here today that I think should be mentioned, namely, the amount per acre below four bushels and

between four and eight bushels. At the present time we are receiving the same rate as when the act was brought into force. With present production costs the amount should be increased considerably because there is no relationship whatever between production costs today and those of ten years ago.
Because we have been asking for a settlement on an individual basis, and because we have agreed in the past to a reduction of the area, the minister may be able to convince his colleagues and also treasury board-I always have difficulty in remembering the name of that organization, because lately I have been thinking of them in different terms, which might not be parliamentary-that we should have what we have been asking for, and what we asked for in committee.
If the minister wishes to use the amendment I moved, members in this group would have no objection whatever. He would have our wholehearted support.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO ELIGIBLE AREAS
speechtext:
The minister replied to the two matters I brought to his attention. In regard to the emergency situation in Saskatchewan, apparently there is to be no increase in the amount per acre allowed under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, nor any change in the policy heretofore existing whereby responsibilities in connection with seed wheat and seed grain rest upon the provinces.

As I understand it, if we had a system of individual payments, under our constitution, that would have to be the responsibility of the provinces. This amendment will make it possible to give assistance to more farmers who have little or no crops while fewer farmers who have crops will receive smaller payments than they have formerly received. The hon. member for Assiniboia seems to be worrying about where the member for Maple Creek stands on this question. There should be no doubt about that whatsoever. speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: FOREST PROTECTION AND EXPERIMENT, CONTROL AND MANAGEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock I had just been speaking of the nature of the forest fires we have been experiencing in this country, and I was pointing out the different types of fires that are encountered. The largest percentage of fires is caused by carelessness of some kind. That carelessness is not something which simply affects the people who may be immediately in contact with whoever has been careless; the consequences may be very far-reaching.
While we are dealing with the bill before us at the present time, I should like to take this occasion to make the suggestion that consideration should be given to an amendment to the Criminal Code to provide adequate penalties for those who carelessly start these fires. At the present time section 513 of the Criminal Code provides penalties for those who wilfully set fire to forests or to other areas, but I believe the penalties connected with this type of carelessness should go beyond wilfully setting fire to forest areas. In the case of people carrying firearms penalties are provided for those who handle weapons recklessly or in such a way that damage may be caused as the natural or reasonable result. As to forest fires, the extent of the damage that may be caused in this way, and the actual threat to life as well, is so great that in examining the whole problem I think consideration should be given to a provision under which people could be adequately punished where there was actual reckless disregard of the safety of the forests, and consequently the safety of other people and of immensely important property.
I mention fires because this is a particular field in which there can be effective co-operation between the dominion and provincial governments. I doubt if there is any single problem connected with our forests today in which there is such a wide divergence between the different provinces as to the facilities available for fire protection under the control of the provincial departments. Under such agreements as may be worked out within the terms of the bill, there are possibilities that I should like to place before the minister which I think may have far-reaching results in dealing with this great problem.

At the present time some provinces have extensive arrangements for constant supervision of the forest areas by means of air patrol. Some have no such arrangements at all. The fire hazard varies, of course, in different provinces according to the type and concentration of the forest areas, but in every province there are areas which require supervision. The cost of maintaining and servicing an adequate air fleet for this purpose is undoubtedly too great for some provinces; and if there is to be provision for air patrol worked out by arrangement between the dominion government and the provinces, then I suggest that consideration be given the possibility of a general plan of air supervision which might be provided in co-operation with the Royal Canadian Air Force. The type of flying that would be done undoubtedly would provide excellent training for many pilots over those areas where they might be called upon to fly under service conditions. At the present time the Royal Canadian Air Force is doing mapping in some of the northern parts of the country. That work, and the type of skill required, would be somewhat similar to air patrols such as I have mentioned, and I believe consideration might well be given to having this type of work done under arrangement with the provinces by one organization that would be brought into service in this way.
Two types of air service are required to do an effective job. One is the constant watch for the outbreak of fire; the other is the actual fighting of the fire once it is discovered. Once a fire has been discovered it is of the utmost importance that aircraft be available, heavy enough to carry to the area as quickly as possible fire-fighting equipment such as pumps and many other items, together with men to fight the blaze. In the discussion of this subject I think consideration might well be given to the organization of two separate groups, one of which would carry out patrols for the purpose of spotting fires as soon as they occurred, the other an organization which for want of a better word might be called air commandos, who would be ready to go into any area and be dropped by parachute with pumps and various other firefighting equipment which would enable them to deal with a fire at the earliest possible moment.
I mentioned the different causes of forest fires for a particular reason, in addition to my desire to emphasize the carelessness that causes many of them. I think many hon. members will be surprised to learn the high percentage of fires caused by lightning. Almost invariably those fires start on high, inaccessible ground, which is where lightning usually strikes. Often these fires will start
Canada Forestry Act
in old, dry stumps on top of a hill, which may be some considerable distance from the nearest place where water may be pumped by hose. It may take a considerable time to reach that point, and in the time it takes men to get there the fire may gain considerable headway, particularly if the forest is dry and a wind is blowing. This suggests the use of equipment with which it would be difficult for any single province to carry out the necessary experiments at the present time. I believe there would be a great chance of stopping many fires before they spread too far if we had an adequate number of helicopters well placed across the country, so that when a fire was spotted on inaccessible high ground a helicopter could go in and drop men, or perhaps put out the fire itself by the use of chemical bombs. Successful experiments already have been carried out along this line, which have demonstrated that a great deal can be done in this way. The employment of modern methods like these, however, require a much larger airborne fire-fighting force than can be maintained by any single province, and I should think this would be one of the most useful fields of discussion when dealing with this problem on a broad basis.
Another field for co-operation, in which the association between the dominion and provincial governments can be very useful, is in the inventory of forest areas by aerial photography. At the present time the province of Ontario has almost completed such an inventory of its total forest area through a system of photography similar to that carried out in mapping operations. Together with the necessary ground examination, this makes it possible to get an exact inventory of the amount of timber of every kind available for development. At the present time there is an agreement between the federal department and the department of lands and forests in Ontario under which the provincial government is doing the actual air photography and those photographs are being turned over to the dominion government, which is producing them in the form of maps that will provide all the essential information from which a complete inventory can be made. That, I should think, would be extremely useful in every province of Canada.
The other field in which co-operation can be most effective is that of research. Tremendous damage has been done our forests through insect infestation on a very large scale. It may be a question as to whether these insect epidemics have not caused as much damage as fire itself. Throughout the Gaspe peninsula today, for instance, you can see dead birch trees which obviously have

Canada Forestry Act
been killed by insect infestation. Throughout great stretches of Ontario you can see dead spruce which have been killed by spruce bud-worm infestation. In other parts of Canada other types of trees have been killed by other insects, such as the sawfly. There is a great opportunity for research in that field.
As a layman, I cannot help wondering whether some of these things are not the result of the unbalance that man creates in nature. I cannot help wondering whether nature does not step in when one type of tree is taken out and other types are left standing; because you generally see these epidemics start in areas in which particular types have been heavily cut. It may well be that this is simply an expression of nature's attempt to restore the balance of trees which originally grew in those areas.
In any event, whatever the background is, these epidemics are recurring ones. The recent spruce budworm epidemic was not the first we have had. We have had serious epidemics in recurring periods for many years. There have been other epidemics as well. If through the research that is being carried out, and which the minister indicates is to be extended by co-operation with the provincial department, these epidemics can be stopped, many millions of dollars' worth of valuable timber will be saved; but what is more, the basis of employment of many thousands of men will also be preserved as a result of that research.
It will not be the role of the department to deal directly with such matters as types of cutting and things of that kind because those are essentially under the provincial governments. Nevertheless, the matter will come up for discussion because the type of cutting and the way in which the slash is left will have a bearing on fire protection and on the other things that will undoubtedly come under the joint supervision of the various governments.
In dealing with this question it is essential that real education in regard to the forest problem be given to our people generally throughout the whole country. Much of what is said publicly is often based upon some particular interest. I can recall some of the strongest statements made upon forest conservation by those who had a direct interest in some particular type of forest exploitation. I know that some of the most appealing statements in regard to preventing some particular type of cutting in favour of another type of cutting have been put forward by the worst timber pirates we had in this country. I mention this fact in connection with this measure because it is extraordinary the attention that is sometimes paid

to statements which are made by those who have a particular axe to grind. I know that those who live in the forest areas have had some experience in this respect.
On the other hand, there are those who are earnestly trying to deal with this problem. The minister has mentioned the important contributions which have been made to an understanding of this vital question, including the report prepared by General Kennedy dealing with this subject in the province of Ontario and the report prepared by Chief Justice Sloan in British Columbia, dealing with the problems in that province. Each of those reports applies fairly generally to the whole problem throughout Canada. By co-operation, many of the recommendations that are put forward in those reports can be carried out across Canada under agencies that might be set up through the joint action of these governments.
I should just like to repeat that I believe one of the greatest opportunities presented by this bill is that of working out a system of adequate air supervision of our forest areas and the setting up of a highly-organized, mobile force of air commandos who will be able to go into any area that is threatened, without any regard to provincial boundaries and who, upon the report by the wireless of the district of a fire that requires attention of this kind, will be able to bring men from strategic points in that area and deal with it before it has spread out and become a menace to the standing timber which is of immense value to our economic future, or before it threatens or in fact destroys whole communities, as they have been destroyed in the past.
I should think this bill would commend itself to every hon. member. Employed in a spirit of co-operation with the provincial governments across Canada, this bill may be the beginning of a solution to a problem which has been causing great concern to everyone. If an effective method of dealing with fire and an effective method of dealing with these epidemics can be worked out, then we can really hope for the ideal of a perpetual supply of forest products for the industries that are based on that great source of raw material.

speechtext:
When we were debating this measure in the resolution stage, Mr. Speaker, as was quite proper, nearly all of the members from British Columbia took part in the debate. I did not do so at that time, partly because so many spoke and partly because I knew there would be another opportunity. As the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) has said, this is a measure which is welcomed by every member of this house; and the greater the understanding that hon. members have of what

forests mean to Canada and of what the liquidation of those forests means, no matter how that liquidation may take place, the more they will welcome the measure.
If I may say so without having the minister think that I am being critical, this is indeed a measure that is long overdue. I am not saying this to criticize the minister now for bringing in the measure or to suggest that he or the government were delinquent in their duty in not bringing it in before. If there is blame, I imagine it is blame we must all share.
Perhaps the people of no other country in the world inherited so vast a forest wealth as the first people who came to this country. In every province from the Atlantic to the Pacific there was a great deal of forest land. Perhaps the magnitude of our forests is some excuse for our disregard of its protection. When our ancestors came to this country and settled in the Atlantic provinces, and in the two central provinces, the forest was indeed considered an enemy. It was something that had to be subdued or destroyed before they could begin to make their clearings on which they expected to produce the food necessary for their existence. The unfortunate part of it is that this attitude remained long after the time when there was sufficient land available for the growing of food.
As I said, every province had its forest wealth. Every province, too, has large areas that are unsuitable for producing anything but forests. This is even true of my own native province of Prince Edward Island, where perhaps every acre can be cultivated. Yet, even in that province, large areas of land are so poor that they should never have been cleared of trees. Many of these sections are now reverting to forests because the land has been left fallow. In my opinion one of the first things that should be undertaken under this measure is a survey to ascertain the land that is suitable for the growing or production of nothing else but forest of some kind.
All provinces have an interest in forest conservation. But my own province of British Columbia has the greatest interest in conservation, as I shall show in a moment. In that province a very small amount of the land area is suitable for agricultural production. A few years ago I saw a report of a speech by the chief forester of British Columbia. He referred to forest surveys that were made during the past thirty-five or forty years. The first survey was about 1910, and the forest cut at the time was about one billion board feet, and it was estimated that we had a forest reserve sufficient to last us for three hundred years. In another ten or fifteen
Canada Forestry Act
years another survey was made and at that time we were cutting about two billion board feet a year, and the estimated duration of the forest reserve had dropped in the interval to about a hundred and fifty years. Shortly after that we had another survey made and the annual cut had risen to about three billion board feet and the reserve had dropped to between thirty and fifty years. That indicates the terrific pace at which the forests of British Columbia have been, and up to the present time are being, liquidated. That is one of the things that I hope this measure will put an end to.
I do not exactly know how they measure it, but the total land area in British Columbia is said to be about 234 million acres. In figures that I received from the department of lands and forests the land has been classified as follows: About 75 million acres, or one-third of the total area, is good forest land. About another 82 million acres, approximately another third, is scrub forest land. Then there is another third, about 72 million acres, which is mountain top, barren, swamp and water. What I should like hon. members to note is that out of that total area of 234 million acres only 4-7 million acres is agricultural land, about 2 per cent of the total. It is no wonder then that the people of British Columbia are what one might call forest conscious. We realize the importance of the forests to us and how essential our forests are to the wellbeing of our people.
However, despite the importance of our forests to our people, up until recent years we have squandered them with reckless abandon. In that regard I do not suppose we have been any more prodigal with our forest reserves than the other provinces. But there is this difference: after our forest is taken away we are not as fortunate as some other provinces. With us there is no arable land left that can be used for the growing of food.
Since Chief Justice Sloan made the report referred to this morning by the minister, a start has been made to change from this rapid liquidation and substitute for it a plan of forest control. How effective it will be I do not know. One of the difficulties suggested to me by people who ought to know is the large amount of money required for the various aspects of conservation. So far as the provincial government is concerned, the revenue they receive from forests is direct and it shows up, as the saying is, like a sore thumb. But the federal government gets several times as much revenue out of the forests of British Columbia in an indirect way, such as income and corporation taxes. I am bound to say, however, that during the last few years the provincial government, even by direct means, should have got more

Canada Forestry Act
of the forest wealth than they did. These figures before me, and they are authentic, show an increase in the value of forest products from $88 million in 1939 to $364 million in 1948. I am satisfied that if the provincial government had gone about it they could have obtained a larger amount of money directly for forest conservation than they did obtain, and particularly in the last few years.
I would hope that through this measure British Columbia would receive through the federal government a portion of the large amount of revenue which comes from the exploitation of the forest wealth of that province. I think I need say nothing further. When I first thought of speaking I had thought I would make a more extended speech. But much of what I intended to say has been said by members who have preceded me, and some of it by the minister himself. I would conclude by saying that I hope the minister now in charge of the bill, or whatever minister may be in charge of it, will take seriously this matter of forest conservation. I hope he will realize that we have not much time, and that the process of rehabilitation, even when carried out with energy, is going to be a long, tedious and expensive task.

Mr. Speaker, I shall take only a few moments to draw your attention to the program of reforestation already carried out, which I do not believe has received proper recognition by the house.
Last spring we welcomed Newfoundland to the Dominion of Canada. In the reading room of the House of Commons we see on the the walls the design of a tree which represents the former nine provinces, and the Yukon. I submit another tree should be planted in that forest that is Canada, so that Newfoundland may have the recognition that is her due.
May I offer my congratulations to the minister upon the introduction of the bill. While it may be late, it is not too late. It has been estimated that the fire and insect loss to forests in Canada runs to something like 800 million cubic feet a year. It has also been estimated that the wastage from logging and sawmill industry operations runs to something over 900 million cubic feet a year, which is greater than the fire and insect loss.
Something should be done to control the wastage brought about by these industries. I cannot add much to the debate, because it seems to me practically everything has been said. The program of reforestation is vital to the agricultural areas of western Canada. Experiments have been carried out in the United States where they placed a line of timber across the dustbowl, as a result of which it was found that the lands in that area have not only been brought back into production but the flood hazards of the Mississippi have been lessened.
I believe we would do well to use the Scandinavian countries and Germany as a model in any reforestation program we might undertake. In addition to the wastage of valuable timber land each year, we must also consider the wildlife in those forests. The trapping industry in Canada is something over $20 million a year, and hunting and trapping licences bring in a revenue of about $4 million, with the additional $100 million from tourist traffic.
With all these in mind I submit the following items should be considered:

Surveys should be carried out to increase our knowledge of the forest inventory. This could be done both on the ground and by aircraft.
Sustained yield forest management should be applied.
Further efforts should be made to control loss by fire, insects and disease.
Forest operators should be rigidly controlled and allowed to cut only mature trees.
An extensive reforestation program should be enforced and attempts made to cut down sawmill waste.
An educational program should be instituted to encourage a greater feeling of responsibility on the part of the public.
This is all I have to say at the present time, but I do want to congratulate the minister and say that I hope this is only a beginning of greater co-operation in this respect between the dominion and provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, first may I say that I think this bill is timely; in fact I think that someone should have had the foresight to have introduced a bill of this nature into this house some thirty years ago. Thirty years ago last February I started some timber operations of my own. Shortly afterward the industry ran into a slump and certain areas were not cut to the extent that we ordinarily would have cut. Many of the trees were considered to be too small to cut. I happened to get the deed to a small area and it might be interesting to hon. members to know that since that time I have taken off two crops of timber. We kept out the fire and we did not cut too small and therefore were able to do that.
Under the regulations governing timber permits in Ontario you cannot cut under thirteen inches at the stump, six inches at the top and a two-log tree. I think those are good regulations and if they are carried out my experience is that you will be able to crop each timber berth about every 25 years.
Forest protection and conservation is not just a matter of keeping out fire or planting new trees. Many other things enter into this matter, such as water conservation. The public should be educated to a greater extent in fire prevention, timber conservation and so on. A reforestation plan is being carried out in my own area and a number of the operators have been planting trees during the past few years. The provincial government has made a practice of plowing up the ground before planting new trees, but my experience has been that the trees grow better when planted in underbrush or where there are
Canada Forestry Act
smaller trees. Some means should be devised under this legislation, probably next year or the year after, for taking over certain areas that have been cut and replanting them rather than clearing up fields for replanting.
It is necessary that we retain our forests if we are to conserve our water. The levels of lake Michigan, lake Huron and Georgian bay are down some 20 feet. Some people blame this on the Chicago water steal, but in my opinion the water just is not coming from the inland lakes. In my country the inland lakes are not filling up as they used to, and the levels of the streams are getting lower each year. The great concrete dams that were built, I suppose by the Department of Public Works, a number of years ago are not filling up. I am reminded of the farmer who died and left his son with a good farm and large buildings. But the son did not take care of the farm and soon he had no grain to put in his barns. That is what has happened to these dams that were built many years ago. I know of many small streams in which speckled trout used to be found but today they dry up in the summer. This is especially true in those areas which have been cut over, where too small trees have been cut or wheffe fire has prevailed.
The minister stated that there are five laboratories in operation, but apparently they have been lax in their operations or perhaps they did not have sufficient equipment. Somfe 20 years ago all the tamarack in this country died and no one knew why, and no one knows yet why that happened. In the last two or three years our balsam trees have been dying. As you drive along the highway you will notice them all red. Neither the dominion nor the provincial laboratories have been able to tell us whether this is due to a grub or to a disease.
Then we have the sawfly menace, the bud-worm menace and the pinworm menace, and so far we have received very few facts about these dangers to our timber. The pinworm bores a hole just about the size of a pin, hence its name, but it operates in sawn lumber as well as in trees. In an effort to counteract this the lumbermen use a poisonous dip but this affects the hands of the workers, especially if they have become scratched. I do not know the best way to handle this, but I think the dominion government should work with the provinces and develop a program of reforestation and research.
This legislation is a step in the right direction and if properly followed up can prove to be a major step, not only in the conservation but in the development of the resources

Canada Forestry Act
of this country. In addition to what is provided by this legislation, efforts should be extended by all governments to align public opinion behind a forestry conservation program. The agricultural and hydro-power development industries of this nation have a vital stake in the forests of the country. Although only indirectly related to forestry, these industries are directly affected by any disturbance of the natural balance of the soil vegetation and water levels. The interdependence of a sound forest conservation program and the progress of electric power development in this country in itself justifies the provisions of this legislation.
In addition to conservation 1 should like to see the government next year-if not next year, as soon as possible-by means of the research facilities which it now possesses extend greatly the research in the field of greater utilization of the so-called weed species. There exists today a big field for the greater utilization of logging and saw mill waste. In the ordinary saw mill operation sawdust represents six to eight per cent of the timber handled. Then the timber blocks and other waste must be taken care of. Many mills in Ontario, and I think this applies to British Columbia and some parts of Quebec, burn all the slabs produced. The use of electricity and gas has reduced the use of slabs for home use, and today they are being either buried or burned.
At the present time I believe there is a shortage of trees for planting on waste farm lands in some areas of Canada. I know this to be a fact in Ontario because in planting trees myself each year I have not been able to secure enough from the forestry department of the province to plant the number of trees I would have liked to. I have been getting quite a few, however, and probably they are developing more, although I do not know. I suggest to the minister that some plan of that sort should be worked out in conjunction with the provinces, or by the dominion alone. As public opinion becomes more conservation conscious, it is only natural to expect the demand for young trees will increase, and I suggest early action be taken to assure an adequate supply of trees for reforestation.
Aside from secondary incomes derived from the forests by means of trapping, tourist trade and water power, this industry yields in excess of a billion dollars annually. Unfortunately the amount of money put back into the industry to conserve these resources has been very little. I should like this legislation to be a forerunner of action that will result in $50 million a year being put back into the industry by the federal and provincial governments, and the industries directly and

indirectly concerned. That is all I have to say on the bill at the present time. I am very much in favour of it.

I want to bring to the attention of the minister and his technicians, perhaps more to them than anyone else, a statement which I found a few days ago in a book entitled "The Coming Age of Wood". It reads:
Wood is inexhaustible. The forest is not a mine that eventually will be depleted, but a crop land. Provided-
The emphasis is on the proviso.
-trees are harvested as a crop and the forest is sustained by proper management, wood will forever yield all the material the human race can conceivably require.
The author undertakes to prove the proposition which he enunciates in the first chapter. He certainly does so to my satisfaction, and I believe to the satisfaction of any person who may care to investigate the book.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to take up much of the time of the house in discussing this subject. I think everyone approves of the bill and is in accord with its principles. Coming as I do from the province of New Brunswick, we are naturally very much interested in lumbering and forestry conservation. Lumbering is one of our most important industries, and when it is not in a prosperous condition the people of New Brunswick are not prosperous. The enemies of forestry conservation have been mentioned, and I think probably man could be named as the first. I think he has done more to destroy the forests of Canada, as he has in other lands, than all the bud-worms and other pests that we could mention. Nevertheless I am sure he is slowly learning the necessity of conserving this great gift.
Some forty-five or fifty years ago it was realized in our educational institutions, and particularly in the university of New Brunswick, that it was necessary that people should

receive more education so far as forestry is concerned. At the university of New Brunswick in the city of Fredericton, we established the first forestry school in Canada. That school has prospered for the last forty-five years. Graduates from the university of New Brunswick have gone to all parts of Canada, the United States and many parts of Europe to assist in the work of reforestation and the spreading of a general knowledge of forestry.
One of the members from British Columbia spoke a few minutes ago about the chief forester of that province. The first chief forester of the province of British Columbia, Mr. Caverhill, was a graduate of the university of New Brunswick. The present chief forester of British Columbia, Mr. Orchard, is also a graduate of the same university. I say these things to indicate the work that has been done. I might also say that the firm of Price Brothers of the province of Quebec, a large lumber concern, for the past number of years has been giving scholarships at the forestry school and sending students to that university. Just last year five scholarships were given in Great Britain for forestry training, and the students were sent to the university of New Brunswick.
I quite agree with what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said this afternoon, that it is most difficult for the smaller provinces to properly protect their forests from fires. I think the suggestion he made that we might use aeroplanes and helicopters is a good one. In many parts of the province of New Brunswick we have now established fire towers, and they have been of great benefit in spotting fires and directing fire fighters to the vicinity in a short time. I also think further education is needed. I was greatly interested a short time ago to read in the February number of a publication issued by the Canadian Forestry Association an article suggesting that more Canadian films should be used to educate our people in forest conservation and similar matters. The article reads:
Motion pictures as an aid to forestry education are an important medium employed by the Canadian Forestry Association. During 1948, Canadian Forestry Association's own motion picture and lecture tours, its film libraries and co-operative tours recorded an attendance in all Canadian provinces of 400,000 men, women and youths, French and English.
They go on to say:
It is regrettable to report that all the major motion pictures, in the 1948 program, dealing with forest management, forest protection, soil erosion, water and wild life were purchased by Canadian Forestry Association in the United States and adapted (and translated for Quebec) in Canada.
The principal producer of forest conservation films on this continent is the United States department of agriculture.
Canada Forestry Act
This article goes on to suggest that the Canadian film board might very properly take a prominent part in the production of such films. I offer that to the minister as a suggestion which I believe should be given careful consideration.
I was interested in the remarks of the last speaker and also those of the hon. member for Victoria, Ont. (Mr. Hodgson) with respect to the use of lumber by-products such as sawdust, slabs and so on. I should like to direct attention to the efforts in this connection of a former member of this house, Mr. J. L. O'Brien, in Northumberland county, New Brunswick. Mr. O'Brien has installed equipment and developed a process at his plant on the Miramichi river by means of which not only the sawdust but the slabs and even the bark are used. In other words he is using one hundred per cent of the log. This is more or less of an experiment, on which Mr. O'Brien is spending a good deal of his own money, but he believes it will be successful. If such a method can be developed by him I am sure it can be used in the industry right across Canada. It is interesting to note that in the past only fifty per cent of a log has been used, with the slabs, the sawdust and the waste making up the other fifty per cent. That is a tremendous loss, which I hope may be eliminated as a result of the work of the organizations being set up under this legislation.

speechtext:
I take the time of the committee, Mr. Chairman, to speak at this point on this bill because I represent a large number of people who have been particularly interested and concerned with forest conservation for a considerable period of years; in fact I represent a number of people who

have led the way in British Columbia in advocating forest conservation principles. I am also rather anxious to make a few remarks and present a few of my ideas to the committee on this bill because I myself have been particularly interested-I should say that it has been a hobby of mine since 1909-in the preservation of a tract of timber and its operation on a permanent yield basis.
I have read this bill carefully and I am pleased to note that it contains some substance and provides the machinery for this government to do something effective in the future in the field of forest conservation. In passing I must say that I listened with great interest this morning to the minister's statement on the second reading of this bill and was pleased indeed to hear in that statement of the intentions of the government and of its plans in connection with this bill.
Some people are considered to be patriots because they wave the flag and make a show by outward and visible demonstration of their loyalty to a country. But in my opinion a person who makes every effort to see that the actual resources of a country are preserved, in forests, in soil and in water, is fulfilling one of the first requirements of being a patriot and a true citizen.
Since the resolution was first introduced I find that support for this bill is widespread. I have had a number of letters from constituents who are interested in the forest industry and who have expressed great pleasure at seeing this bill come before the house. In reading the press and various magazines I have also noticed that there is a great deal of outspoken support for the government's purpose as expressed in this bill.
In dealing with this question of the conservation of our forests, we have three important questions to ask:	What is our present
position, what is our objective, and how can we attain that objective? Before making a few personal suggestions as a result of experience in British Columbia, I am first of all going to deal briefly with the situation as it is in that province, because naturally I am better informed on conditions there than on conditions elsewhere; and having been a member of the provincial legislature of British Columbia for some years, I have followed with great interest the work and have had quite a close association with some of the forestry officials of that province.
In order to proceed with my argument I find myself repeating three sets of figures that were given by a previous member, but I do so in order to give a true picture while speaking at this time. We find that the total

land area of British Columbia is 234,403,000 acres. The land area capable of producing commercial timber is about 75 million acres, although included in that figure is some land that might only produce marginal timber. The area of land which is incapable of producing commercial timber is 154,678,000 acres; agricultural land, 4,702,000 acres. That means that we have 32 per cent of the total area which is capable of producing timber of some type; 66 per cent is incapable of producing commercial timber and 2 per cent of the land area of British Columbia is suitable for agricultural purposes. From those figures hon. members can clearly understand the great importance of the forest industry to British Columbia.
From the latest figures I have been able to obtain, it is estimated that there is at present 280 billion feet of accessible timber in British Columbia. When I say "accessible", that is a rather relative term because it changed with the introduction of machinery. By that I mean timber that can be taken out with modern equipment at a profit at this time. Timber which is now accessible was considered strictly inaccessible when I was a boy when it had to be hauled by horses for a long distance.
The main causes of forest depletion are logging, destruction by fire, insect pests, diseases and what we term windthrows. I am interested to note that according to the latest figures I can get for British Columbia the depletion by logging in that province averages 3J billion board feet per year. That is the consumption of our timber resources on account of logging. The depletion by fire averages 300 million board feet per year. The depletion from insects and disease averages over 400 million board feet per year. The total annual depletion of our accessible forest wealth in British Columbia at the present time is nearly 4J billion board feet. That is an impressive figure.
Chief Justice Sloan, in his report relating to the forest resources of British Columbia, published in 1945-to anyone who is interested in a careful study of forest resources, I would recommend the reading of that report- estimated on the basis of the present rate of depletion that the coast stands of timber would last as follows:

From these figures, Mr. Chairman, you can see that the interior of British Columbia represents a much better picture than does the coast area.
These figures that I have given illustrate the British Columbia situation clearly and I think they are indicative generally of the position with respect to our forests in Canada as a whole.
For a few moments I want to deal with the question of utilization. As we understand it, logging waste is the proportion of the tree that has marketable value which is left in the woods, such as sound logs, butts, breakages and unused tops. From a study made in 1932 by J. H. Jenkins and F. W. Guernsey, it was found that nearly 20 per cent of merchantable timber was left in the woods of British Columbia as logging waste. This alone means that 750 million feet of merchantable timber is wasted in the woods each year in British Columbia. I therefore suggest that there is a great opportunity here for the federal and provincial governments to carry out experiments similar to what was termed the Ladysmith experiment conducted by the Comox Logging and Railway Company, the Powell River Company and the British Columbia provincial forest service. In my opinion the solution to this question will mean the establishment of new grades for recovered material and concessions to logging operators and lumber companies so far as royalty and stumpage are concerned.
I want to deal very briefly with saw mill waste. The fact that about 20 per cent of the wood volume per acre is now being wasted during logging operations must lead us to consider what happens to 80 per cent of a tree that arrives in a mill. A study of fourteen different coast mills by the same company, J. H. Jenkins, in 1928 revealed the fact that about 30 per cent of Douglas fir logs and 33 per cent of hemlock logs were lost in the slabs, edgings and sawdust. They lost approximately 30 per cent in the manufacturing plus 20 per cent in logging. That means about 50 per cent of the volume of the

Canada Forestry Act
trees cut in British Columbia are lost in logging and manufacturing. By the time they arrive at the mill there is a further loss owing to the uneconomic utilization of logs through poor equipment. There is quite a place, Mr. Chairman, for a study by the federal government or by co-operation between the two governments, of the use of proper equipment in the cutting of timber in this country. Then again there is a further loss through the lack of markets for low grades and from the lack of use of, shall I say, by-products left in the bush.
What I mean by the lack of markets because of the failure to utilize low grades I could illustrate in this way. When the trimmer saws are operating in the saw mills you very often see two by fours, two by sixes or other dimensions of timber cut from a log having a slight wane on one corner, which prevents it being used for house building, and as a result of this wane one often sees two feet, four feet or six feet of this dimension timber trimmed and wasted.
If we were utilizing our timber properly as they are in Great Britain and Scandinavia that two by four or two by six or any dimension of that type could be used in such buildings as garages, or outside structures where you do not intend to use any interior sheeting.
Then, Mr. Chairman, there is a considerable loss of timber in the use of high-grade logs for dimension timber, and so on, owing to the variations in the market and the lack of experience. I have visited a number of small mills and portable mills and have found, for instance, No. 1 cedar logs being cut up for two-inch and three-inch cedar planks or No. 1 Douglas fir logs being cut into shiplap and material of that type, when those fir logs should be used entirely for fir flooring, furniture materials and high-grade lumber. Therefore I wish to make a few suggestions to the minister for his consideration to promote the greater utilization of logs. I suggest it would be an excellent thing for the government to investigate the possibilities for more efficient types of saw mill equipment to overcome the present loss of timber caused by the inserted tooth saw. We have the inserted tooth saw and the solid saw. The reason the inserted tooth saw is used is that it is much easier for the average man to use. It does not require a skilled man to sharpen the saws, skilled mechanics and so on. The inserted tooth saw causes an excessive amount of waste in sawdust when sawing. Also inefficient carriages and wasteful edging cause losses. There is no question about it. Anyone who has followed the lumber industry in this country throughout the years, particularly the smaller mills and the portable mills, will realize how little advancement we
[Mr. Herridge.l
have made in efficient sawing equipment, especially when we compare it with the advances that have been made in other directions so far as machinery is concerned. I would suggest to the minister that there is a great opportunity there for a study of saw mill equipment, particularly as it applies to small mills and portable mills. I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that further study of the utilization of saw mill waste for the manufacture of furniture, household equipment and box materials could be given serious consideration.
Anyone who has been associated with the lumber industry will realize that possibly the greatest amount of waste occurs in the smaller mills or in the portable mills where the owners are unable to use that waste because of being some distance from the local market and because of the lack of capital to purchase these things that are required to utilize the waste, the machinery and so on. That is a subject which could well be studied.
I have not seen the machines but I have been told that in Scandinavia, in parts of Germany, and in other parts of Europe there are in use, or were in use previous to the last war, some very efficient saw mill equipment operated on the band saw principle which can be operated with very low power. In the lumber industry power cost is one of the chief obstacles to the small mill operator. The small chap who has a small timber holding or who buys his logs from wood lots on the farms, or has small timber holdings which he operates, finds that power is one of the bugbears. I suggest that the minister's department could give serious consideration to investigating these types of saw mills, which are of the band saw type. I have been told by a lumber operator that in Sweden they have a type of band saw which is utilized in this way. The farmer takes a two-foot log, puts it on the carriage and heads it into a series of small band saws. He then goes and milks the cows, does his chores, goes to bed, and gets up in the morning and the machinery is so timed that he would have a couple of dozen inch planks ready for farm use. I think that should receive some attention from the minister's department because it would be a great help to farmers in this country, and particularly to small lumber operators, to be able to cut lumber with low powered engines.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the department give consideration to the development of the co-operative purchase of machinery between small mills. The trouble is that waste occurs because there are, as in my own district, dozens of small operators wasting a high percentage of the log after it reaches the mill, in addition to the woods waste, because they have not the capital to purchase this machinery. I suggest that some consideration should

be given to the co-operative purchase of processing plants, and to getting firms interested in the building of centralized processing plants in which the waste from a number of portable mills could be taken and processed. I suggest that the minister's department could very well investigate the possibilities of markets for by-products. Our timber has been so plentiful until recent years that I am of the opinion not sufficient serious consideration has been given to the question of by-products from the lumber industry. Consideration of assistance should be given toward the cost of transportation of these products to markets. In some districts particularly that might mean the introduction of special rates by the railroads or shipping companies, as a result of government intervention. That may seem a sort of unusual suggestion, but I can illustrate. In my district, if we had a special rate for say cord-wood going from the Arrow lakes to the city of Trail at a lower rate than the present rate it would be a great help. At the present time you can barely ship wood to cover the cost. If there was a lower rate in effect for that wood, that is a rate of say $10 a car less, small operators would be induced to use up a great deal of timber which is now left in the bush to rot. I advance that as another suggestion to the minister's department.
Then there is the question of consideration of tax concessions to promote the greater utilization of timber in the woods and at the saw mill by both the federal and provincial governments. While on the surface this may appear to mean a temporary loss of revenue to the federal or provincial government, I maintain that if we are able to utilize our natural resources to much greater advantage it is in the end a total gain to the community.
I wish now to discuss several aspects of forest protection. I have been interested in the subject for many years. In my time I have done a good deal of fire fighting, and I could tell some most interesting stories as a result of my experiences. However, I shall not do that but shall confine my remarks to the subject at hand because, Mr. Chairman, I must tell you that I live in great fear of you.
There has been a great improvement in this respect in British Columbia in recent years owing to the increase in the use of aircraft, lookouts and suppression crews in fire fighting. I say that the government of British Columbia and the forest service of that province deserve a great deal of credit. I have seen that service develop throughout the years to a point where it has now become particularly efficient.
I believe it was before lunch that the leader of the opposition suggested that there could be co-operation between the Royal
Canada Forestry Act
Canadian Air Force and the forest services of the various provinces with a view to having the R.C.A.F. patrol for forestry purposes. That may be possible in some sections of Canada, but I do not think it is possible in British Columbia because it requires the use of a light type of aircraft to travel between the high mountains. It would involve great risk to fly a heavy plane low between mountain peaks, and ranges.
In that connection I suggest there is room for further research as to the types of equipment used in fire fighting. A suggestion was made by a previous speaker which I wish to endorse. He pointed out that the lack of roads and trails into our forest areas had up to the present time constituted one of the biggest handicaps in the matter of successful fire fighting owing to the time taken to reach the point where the fire is actually burning. I do believe something should be done between the federal government and the provinces to extend the roads into forest areas, and where roads are not possible trails so that pack horses could be used.
I further suggest the possibility of a greater use of chemicals in the early stages of fighting forest fires. There is the possibility that that subject might be further investigated, because chemicals are light, can be packed easily and can reach almost inaccessible places. That question should receive further consideration.
I will deal only briefly with the question of the control of insect pests and disease. A great deal of excellent work has been accomplished by the science service of the Department of Agriculture in this connection. I should like to express my appreciation of the work that branch has been doing, because I have come in contact with some of the science service men and the work they have been doing. My suggestion to the minister would be that more funds are required to carry on the necessary work.
Secondly, there should be co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, universities and industry to a much higher degree. More publicity should be given in our universities and schools with respect to this aspect of forest conservation.
I come now to the subject of forest management and silviculture. While federal and provincial officials have given attention to the question of forest management, reproduction, regeneration and the rate of growth, a great deal more will have to be done in this connection before a sound and effective policy is developed.
In that connection, and in order to be as brief as possible, I should like to quote from

Canada Forestry Act
the recommendations of the royal commission on forestry in British Columbia in 1945, headed by Chief Justice Sloan:
The future existence of our forest industries depends upon the intelligent management of our forest land to insure its continued productivity. No industry that continues to deplete the source of its own raw material can hope to survive without providing for the future replenishment of that material.
If our forest heritage is to be preserved instead of destroyed we must think of forest production in terms of renewable crops, not only for the growing of wood, but for the perpetuation of all those manifold benefits which the forest has bestowed upon mankind.
Our basic fundamental and vital forest problem is to see to it that our forests are perpetuated for the use, profit and pleasure of our future generations. If we fail in this objective then the economic future of British Columbia will present a very dark and dismal picture. Fortunately it is not too late to plan now for the future, but the sands are running out and the time is now upon us when the present policy of unmanaged liquidation of our forest wealth must give way to the imperative concept of a planned forest policy designed to maintain our forests upon the principle of sustained yield production. Our forest land must be regarded as a source of renewable crops and not as a mine to be exploited1 and abandoned.
I quote again from the report of the same commission:
In 1910 a royal commission was appointed to inquire into forestry matters in British Columbia and an important recommendation was contained in the report of the commission relative to the forest revenue. It reads as follows:
"Your commissioners regard the income from royalty on timber as differing essentially from any other form of revenue in the province. Such receipts should be regarded as capital-not as current revenue. We have no hesitation in recommending that the amount so received, large as it may appear, should be expended by the government for the protection, conservation, and restoration of our timber resources. With our present knowledge regarding re-afforestation to treat these receipts as other than capital would be utterly unsound in principle and might produce disastrous results in the ultimate impairment of the public estate."
It is regrettable to have to record that for thirty-five years this recommendation has been consistently ignored and disregarded by succeeding governments.
That recommendation was made thirty-five years ago, but until quite recently even the government of British Columbia took no action in that respect. Thirty-five years of neglect! I emphasize this point, because federal and provincial governments draw a large revenue from the forests. A greater percentage of that revenue must be returned for the conservation and protection of our forests, on the part of both the federal government and the provincial governments concerned.
The public estate has suffered impairment during the last thirty-five years from the lack of funds essential to forest management. The public interest requires that this state of affairs should no longer continue.

Ample money must be voted under this act if it is going to have any effective results. I find that in Canada in 1946 there was a total expenditure of $30 million on forest management, research and forest problems. The federal governmnt spent $2 [DOT] 6 million, the provincial governments $10-7 million, and private industry $16-4 million. That makes a total of $30 million. The Canadian Forestry Association recommends that by 1955 we should have a total annual expenditure on forest management in Canada, divided between federal and provincial governments, and private industry, of $100 million.
I should like now to make brief reference to the research carried on by the Vancouver forest products laboratory of the dominion forest service. I recognize the excellent work being done by that laboratory, with its timber mechanics division, its division to investigate utilization and seasoning, wood preservation and timber pathology division and the wood chemistry division. I understand that now they are experimenting with the production of gas from wood and have had some very interesting results, although I am told that at the present time it cannot be produced at an economical price. I give all credit to the men working at the Vancouver forest laboratory, but I should like to criticize the government to the extent of saying that too few people in Canada know just what that laboratory and the other laboratories investigating forest products are doing. I understand that their findings are published in certain trade and lumbermen's journals and a few other publications, but there are hundreds of people operating small mills, logging operations or engaged in educational work who know nothing about the excellent work being done. I suggest that greater publicity should be given to the work of these scientists who are working on our behalf.
If we are going to have a sound, effective policy there should be a widespread educational program. When you discuss these matters with Scandinavians or Europeans or people of the British isles you discover that behind the law is a great consciousness on the part of the people of the necessity for conservation. The spirit of conservation prevails. If we are going to get the co-operation of the Canadian people for the maintenance of government-sponsored forests across this country we must start to educate in the elementary schools and proceed right through to the universities, not forgetting many types of adult organizations.
In addition to forest management and forest conservation, we require an over-all conservation policy because forest conservation

is only one facet of a national conservation program. I suggest that there is great need for an interdepartmental committee on conservation to be made up of forest engineers, agricultural scientists, meteorologists, members of the hydrographic service and other related departments such as the national film board. Conservation should be approached as a whole, not in tidbits.
I recommend to the government that they work in close co-operation with the Canadian Forestry Association, the Canadian Association of Forest Engineers, the Agricultural Institute of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other bodies and organizations of a technical or popular nature that are interested in the development of this program. I do not know to what extent this co-operation exists at the present time, but I believe it is necessary to involve the people in the day-to-day administration of their own affairs if they are going to be administered in a democratic, efficient and effective way.
In conclusion I stress the need for education, organization, co-operation and sufficient funds for the development of a satisfactory and complete conservation program in Canada.

Newfoundland, Canada's tenth and newest province, can show the best all-round record in forest management. Here most of the forest areas are held in perpetuity by the two pulp and paper companies. There has been a minimum of government interference. Unlike the alarming decline in the forests in other parts of Canada, Newfoundland now has considerably more timber than it had fifty years ago.
