Mr. Chairman, I feel, as was said this afternoon, that this measure is probably one of the most important pieces of legislation introduced in the house for many years. As so many have said, that is particularly true because it is so long overdue. I am quite sure the minister will agree with me when I say that it is a great challenge to whatever minister is charged with the responsibility of administering Canada's forest policy. I think it is recognized that forestry is Canada's biggest business, but I often wonder whether the Minister of Finance really appreciates that fact. Many times representatives of the industry have come to Ottawa to discuss taxation policy with the Minister of Finance and his officials, but unfortunately they were never able to establish as good a case of poverty during the prosperous war years as the mines were able to. As a result the officials of the Department of Finance have never given the problem the attention which it certainly merits.
I should also like to say to the minister that I hope forestry will not be relegated to a minor branch of some kind within a service under the new departmental set-up that is being inaugurated. I think forestry well merits the recognition of having a branch assigned to it in order that the chief forester of Canada may be able to make his reports direct to the minister rather than through another departmental head who is probably not familiar with the intricate problems involved in forestry. The bill certainly gives ample powers to the minister, and I hope that the forestry department will look around in

Canada and try to accumulate a staff of first-class men, which I can assure him is very difficult to obtain.
I understand that within his department he has one economist working on the problems of forest economics. It is a study and field in which a great deal of pioneering can be done. I was particularly glad to learn from the minister that a man was employed in his department in that capacity. It is also most important that we have taxation studies. Timber is treated altogether differently from any other natural resource in Canada. Under the income tax set-up that has prevailed in the past, it has not been possible for a man to obtain capital gains without taxation if he should happen to own his own timber. The only way a man could make capital gains, if he owned timber over a long period of time, was to get out of the timber business, something that I am sure the minister will agree is most undesirable. In order to take capital gains and get the money that is necessary to replace the timber that he is cutting, it has been necessary for him to sell it inasmuch as that was the only way available to him to secure the capital gain.
There is another point that has never been recognized by the taxation department. I refer to the fact that in the timber business, entirely different from anything else, there is an uninsurable risk. There is the danger of fire to the capital timber which one owns, and also the danger of destruction by insects. I am quite sure that if the minister consults the taxation experts in the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue he will find that the timber people of this country have been given no consideration for that very definite expense which they must incur.
In this legislation we are giving the minister power to enter into agreements with the provinces. He can go to a province and say, "We are interested in your problems of fire and insect protection". I would not want to put this on a coercion basis, but if we are going to contribute to the cost of this work by the provinces I believe we should be consulted, let us say, as to their methods of taxation. Certainly there is no use in the timber people applying to the Minister of Finance or the Minister of National Revenue for some lightening of the taxation load, only to have the provincial governments come along and take up whatever slack or relief has been afforded. I believe the taxation of timber and saw mills in Canada should be done on the basis of consultation between the federal and provincial governments.
Canada Forestry Act
Men with a knowledge of forestry and its economics are very scarce in Canada. Most of them have received university training. The only way they can follow their profession is to accept employment with the large companies. Those large companies usually have their own policies, and to a certain degree they can dictate to the foresters what they shall say in regard to reforestation and other economic problems. It must be recognized, of course, that any company employing foresters must exercise reasonable control over them, to see that they do not speak their mind too bluntly on matters having to do with the provincial administration of forests. In discussing this problem with foresters all over the country it has occurred to me that very few of them are free agents. Many would like to get up and speak their minds, but sometimes it is not altogether in the interests of their employers that they should be quite so blunt or brutal as the situation may require. If within the federal forestry structure we could employ some of these really capable men, they would be able to give us first-class, unbiased advice. The federal government, of course, is not primarily interested in royalty revenue; to a great degree its revenue comes in the way of income tax, but I am sure foresters employed by the federal government could give us much better opinions on these problems than it is possible for us to get at the present time.
We often speak of reforestation. I believe one of the most effective ways of seeing that reforestation was carried out in Canada would be to amend the Criminal Code. It should be a criminal offence if, when a man logs a square mile of timber, he does not make arrangements to re-seed it with trees or follow other methods to ensure that a second crop of timber will grow there. I know that sounds like very harsh treatment, but my logging experience has led me to believe that the practices we have followed in the past have resulted in the many thousands of square miles of denuded timber limits we see right across this country.
As far as the utilization of forest products is concerned, I thought the hon. member for Kootenay West offered an excellent suggestion when he said one reason the small operators particularly cannot utilize all the timber products was because they lacked capital. I see we have now moved into the field of loaning large sums of money to the coal industry. I have no doubt that is a very worthy project, but I believe something also could be done for the timber industry. This might be something the forest economists in the minister's department would

Canada Forestry Act
look into. At the present time a pulp mill which will utilize forest waste costs a minimum of $10 million. I would hope that the research branch of the department might explore the possibility of erecting some sort of small plant which would convert the final and complete pulp product, which I believe would be a wonderful contribution. If for the expenditure of $25,000 or $50,000 a process could be worked out which would enable the small operators to utilize the waste which at present they either throw into the water or burn, it would be a wonderful thing.
Another very important matter the research department might well look into is the removal of bark from trees. I was very interested the other day to learn that one of the minister's scientists had discovered a method of doing that, by injecting some liquid into a tree which would cause it to shed its bark within six months. That is a worth-while and useful project, and I would hope that further experiments might be carried out in that regard.
As far as conservation is concerned, I think we all agree that insect and fire control are of paramount importance in this field. So often, of course, people who are not familiar with timber matters assume that we should limit our cutting of mature forests. Personally I think that is a wrong policy. Economically I believe our mature timber in British Columbia, for instance, is perhaps worth more today than it ever will be again. I can see the vast possibilities that lie ahead in the field of metallurgy; and I think probably we should cut our mature timber as we require it. One fact often forgotten is that when a forest is mature it is no longer growing, in which case if you cut it and make sure another crop is planted you are certainly increasing the forest production of Canada.
In conclusion I should like to congratulate the minister on this bill, which gives him a great opportunity to do something really worth-while for Canada; and I am sure he will live up to the challenge.

I suggest to the minister that just as soon as a fire is put out a bulldozer should move in and replanting should commence; otherwise grass grows and another tree comes up that does not belong there at all, so we do not have the forest we want. The idea is that we should replant as quickly as possible. The same thing would apply when some insect pest comes along and

kills a great many of our trees. Let the bulldozer move in and push those trees out of the way. They are no use to anyone; they are simply firewood, and a nuisance. The best thing to do is go ahead and replant in such a way that our soil and water will be conserved. Nature has a wonderful way of doing things that man cannot match.
I want to tell the minister I am very pleased that he is coming in with this bill. It is something that is badly needed; the provinces cannot handle it, while the dominion can. We want reforestation, particularly in those lands that have been burnt over and are no good for anything else. The grass is growing there now, and that grass should be bulldozed off and the area replanted with trees.

speechtext:
I want to thank the minister for his answer. We shall get some interesting information from those studies. While I am on my feet I wish to mention my firm belief in the necessity of building up a national forest protection consciousness as a result of education in the schools. To illustrate, Mr. Chairman, in my own district of Kootenay West years ago before the children were taught these subjects in the schools, before they had lecturers from the Canadian forestry association coming around, there was little thought of the forests with respect to fire; there was little regard for reporting of fires caused by lightning. Today in the interior of British Columbia as soon as lightning causes a fire any child who is old enough lo appreciate it, when he sees the fire, is so conscious of forestry protection that he will go to the nearest telephone or to a person's home and make every possible effort to notify the proper officials so that the department can take action.
As against that we have a large number of tourists who come from the United States cities and our own cities. It is amazing to notice the lack of forest protection consciousness among both the adults and children. They throw cigarettes around in the moss without any realization of the danger. In many instances fires are started in our district-in most instances as far as human agencies are concerned-by people who have lived in the cities and are out camping or fishing or enjoying themselves in the woods and who start fires because they do not understand the necessity for forest protection. I wish to emphasize the necessity of bringing
{Mr. Gibson (Hamilton West).]
that home particularly to the children who are brought up in the cities of this country by education on the need for forest protection.

criticizing it at all. I am just interested in knowing what the reason is for that differentiation. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: The great difference is, of course, that the advances on capital expenditures are made until such time as the market is judged right for floating a loan at advantageous rates, and sufficient sums are accumulated on which to float an issue. For example, the last issue was seventy million dollars floated at 21 per cent. Obviously if the government did not charge some interest on that it would be to the railway's advantage to prolong indefinitely the floating of such a loan for capital expenditures, and so avoid the payment of interest. On the other hand advances, so far as deficits are concerned, are advances against a deficit which is eventually going to be paid by the people of Canada anyway. So there we would be just charging interest to ourselves.

Mr. Chairman, I believe the matter I wish to bring to the attention of the parliamentary assistant is relevant to this section, judging from the marginal note describing it. An evening newspaper contains the following Canadian Press dispatch:
A federal court today ordered the civil aeronautics board to hold up action on the request of Trans-Canada Air Lines for a new route in the United States . . .
The court's action might mean many months' delay in putting into effect a portion of the new civil aviation agreement signed last June 4 by Canada and the United States.
This agreement was signed some months ago. Under it Canada received certain rights from the United States and the United States received certain rights from Canada. Canada has implemented what she promised to do. Apparently however the United States has failed to implement her portion of the agreement. Naturally that is going to affect the revenue of Trans-Canada Air Lines.
Colonial Air Lines by means of a court action are trying to prevent Canada from reaping the benefits of the agreement we signed on June 4. Is the minister or the government prepared to take some action to see that the United States lives up to her part
[Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood) .1
of the agreement? I understand from the newspaper report that the transport board may be summoning Colonial Air Lines to appear before it some time in the future. I hope that will be done, because if one side of an agreement is not kept I do not think the other side should be kept.
I suggest that not only should the contract of Colonial Air Lines be cancelled, but if the United States is not going to carry out her agreement we should cancel her rights at Gander. This is something which should be cleared up tonight before we go any further with this matter affecting Trans-Canada Air Lines.

Young and old, as my friend says. It is a wholesome food product. Someone has just reminded me that the parliamentary assistant was responsible in some measure for bringing in a substitute for some of our good butterfat, thus creating the circumstances under which we are accumulating surpluses. Now he refuses to recognize ice cream as a wholesome food product. He claims it is a dessert, something that is in the same class as jello or some of these other things which have very little food value. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member for Melfort does not quite recall the substance of my argument. My argument was not that ice cream was a dessert so much as the fact that the bulk of ice cream is used as a confection. The figures I have from the national dairy council show that 40 per cent of all the ice cream sold is in the form of cones. Another substantial percentage is sold in the form of sundaes and all these other confections which may be purchased at soda fountains. There is a further use of ice cream, but at the present time it is the smallest one, its use in the home as a dessert. I pointed out at that time that many desserts are still subject to sales tax, and those are articles which are used entirely as desserts and not as a confection. It is for these reasons that the sales tax on ice cream has been continued. So far as the amount is concerned, it has been calculated that the actual sales tax paid on an ice cream cone is one-sixth of a cent.
If that be the case, it should be easy enough to arrange to take the tax off bricks of ice cream and let it remain on bulk.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
That would get back to the very difficult problem of having the retailer sort out what part of his sales are in that form and tax free and what part are over the counter and taxable. That is exactly what I tried to explain to the house we are now seeking to do in this new sales and excise tax structure, to have four easily recognizable groups all levied at the manufacturer's level

Excise Tax Act
in order to avoid the difficulty of collecting the tax at the retail level, and also the annoyance and inconvenience to the retailer himself.

I have listened to the statement that the tax is only one-sixth of a cent on a cone. One-sixth of a cent is not very much, but one-sixth of a cent means a lot to the people who are selling ice cream. If they have to absorb the one-sixth of a cent, and are not making a profit in the sale of ice cream cones, they are going to push some other article instead of ice cream. That is what is happening. The margin has become so narrow for the people who are handling ice cream that they are substituting and pushing some other article. The result is that sales of ice cream are tapering off. We are losing a market for a valuable dairy product, and in another department of the government they are stepping in and paying a subsidy. Where the government is supporting the prices of dairy products, it seems to me it would be only good business for them to remove the sales tax on these products in order to provide a better market for them. That would be just sound business.

speechtext: I could not follow one part of the hon. member's argument. Did I understand him to say that milk sales, that is, all milk, butter, cheese and ice cream, are four times what they were in 1939?

No. The amount of milk used in the production of ice cream in Canada is four times what it was in the 1935-39 period. That was the amount used last year in the making of ice cream, but it is now tapering off.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
As everyone knows, Mr. Chairman, the Industrial Development Bank was incorporated by an act of the Senate and House of Commons in August, 1944. The purpose of this institution, in brief, was to extend financial assistance to small and medium sized industrial enterprises in Canada which might reasonably be expected to prove successful, but which because of their size or other special factors were unable to obtain necessary financing from other lenders on reasonable terms and conditions.
The bank was set up as a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada. Directors of the Bank of Canada are directors of the Industrial Development Bank. The governor of the Bank of Canada is president of the Industrial Development Bank. The share capital of the bank was fixed at $25 million, all subscribed by the Bank of Canada. The Industrial Development Bank may also issue debentures, not guaranteed by the government, up to a maximum of three times its capital and reserve, but no such securities have yet been issued.
At this point, a brief review of the bank's operations during the five years of its existence may be of some interest. In the period up to the end of the Industrial Development Bank's fiscal year on September 30, 1949, the bank had dealt with 1,960 applications for financial assistance. Of these, 613 were withdrawn by the applicants because they had obtained financing elsewhere or for other reasons, and 657 were refused by the bank
(Mr. Sinclair.)
as unjustifiable risks. The number of applications authorized was 690, for a total amount of $46,341,210. Of these credits a total of 437 were still on the books of the bank at September 30, 1949, for a total in current authorized credits of $32,154,946, of which $23,573,729 was actually outstanding at that date.
Of the credits which have been granted by the bank during its five years of operations, 120 had already been repaid in full, involving a total sum of $7,102,613. Including repayments on account, the bank had already been repaid $11,737,746 out of total disbursements amounting to $35,311,475 during this period.
As the annual reports made by the bank to the Minister of Finance show, the bank's loans and investments have been distributed geographically fairly well in the same pattern as total industrial development in Canada.
The last published annual report, as at September 30, 1948, shows that the bank had met its operating expenses out of its income in the four years of operations up to that date and in addition had built up a reserve for losses of $300,000 and a reserve fund of $783,612. Actual bad debts on loans and investments had been very small, amounting to only $34,340 up to that date. The annual report for the bank's fiscal year ending September 30, 1949, together with its audited statements, will not be available until about December 10 next, but it is understood that this good record has been maintained.
As mentioned earlier, the Industrial Development Bank's facilities were expected to be sought mainly by small and medium sized industrial enterprises. To ensure that the major part of the bank's resources would be available for the smaller undertakings, subsection (2) of section 15 of the act of incorporation was included. This subsection had the effect of limiting to $15 million the aggregate amount of financial assistance which the bank could extend in amounts exceeding $200,000 for any one enterprise.
Since 1944, there has been a very considerable increase in the costs involved in projects for industrial capital investment, which is the typical purpose for which Industrial Development Bank credits are made. In consequence, a project which on the basis of 1944 costs would have involved financing from the Industrial Development Bank of less than $200,000 may, under existing conditions, involve substantially more and therefore come within the limitations of subsection (2) of section 15 of the act.
At September 30, 1949, of the $32,154,946 in current authorized credits on the books of the bank, $19,519,801 was in individual credits for amounts not exceeding $200,000 and $12,635,145 was in credits for amounts in

excess of $200,000. Partial repayments on account had reduced the amount of net authorizations over $200,000 to $11,227,888. This type of application is one with which the bank continues to be asked to deal, and would fairly soon result in the $15 million limitation preventing the bank authorizing credits of over $200,000 to industrial concerns which met all the other requirements of the bank and did not have access to reasonable credit facilities elsewhere.
The proposed amendment to subsection (2) of section 15 will relieve this situation by increasing the limitation on credits exceeding $200,000 from $15 million to $25 million. At the same time it is obvious that in view of the fact that the act enables the bank to provide financial assistance up to a total of at least $100 million, an increase from $15 million to $25 million in the limit on loans over $200,000 will not interfere with the granting of smaller credits, since $75 million would be earmarked for that field in comparison with current authorizations of $19,519,801 at September 30, 1949.
It is also recommended that several other minor amendments be made at this time.
One amendment will make it clear that while the bank is an agent of the crown, nevertheless actions may be taken by or against the bank in its own name rather than by proceedings instituted in the name of the Attorney General of Canada or by petition of right against the crown.
Another amendment will permit the bank to make credit available if the board of directors of the bank is satisfied that the applicant is about to undertake an enterprise which is "an industrial enterprise", as defined by the act. Under the present legislation the determination as to whether a particular enterprise is an industrial enterprise would in the final analysis have to be determined by the courts.
Another amendment is to permit the bank to make a loan where money has been invested by some other person in the enterprise so long as the board is satisfied that the amount invested by others affords reasonable protection to the bank. This amendment broadens to some extent the concept of the investment to be considered as junior to the bank's investment.
Another amendment is to clarify the application of one section of the bill concerning the program in the province of Quebec.

The over-all ceiling on loans to be made under the act is set out in section 14, which says that the aggregate of the total direct liability of the bank, and so on, and so on, shall not exceed three times the aggregate amount of the paid-up capital and the reserve fund.
In other words, if the bank has $25 million capital, its total loans could be $75 million; but the loans of $200,000 and up cannot exceed $15 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Now, may I ask a question. When the parliamentary assistant was discussing this phase of the matter earlier-and I think some on this side of the house joined in the suggestion-reference was made to the ceiling being four times the amount of the capital. Section 14 of the act reads:
The aggregate of the total direct liabilities of the bank, including bonds and debentures issued by the bank, and of the total contingent liabilities of the bank in the form of guarantees given or underwriting agreements entered into by it, shall not at any time exceed three times the aggregate amount of the paid-up capital and the reserve fund, for which provision is made hereinafter.
When the parliamentary assistant was speaking earlier tonight he referred to an aggregate total of $100 million and explained that was four times the $25 million, whereas it seems to me it should be only three times the $25 million. In other words, the ceiling is $75 million unless there is something else in there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That reference was to another section of the act under which the bank is authorized to borrow up to three times its capital.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: It adds that to the original $25 million and that is where you get the $100 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: How much has been lent in loans under $200,000? I understand the total loans of $200,000 and over was about $12 million.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: The total of loans of $200,000 and less is $19,519,801.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Apparently one of the purposes of this bill is to increase the amount that can be lent in loans of $200,000 and over.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Yes. There is no change in the provisions affecting loans of $200,000 and under.

Industrial Development Bank Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Will that not mean that there will be that much less available for the smaller loans?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: There is a ceiling of $75 million for loans of all sizes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: It is $100 million now.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: If the ceiling for loans of $200,000 and over is raised from $15 million to $25 million will that not mean that the amount available for the smaller loans will be reduced by $10 million?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: There will be no change in the discretion of the bank to make loans of less than $200,000 because the money is available now out of profits, reserves and capital funds.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: The money is available for the smaller loans?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: My point is that the total that could be let out in the way of small loans would be reduced by $10 million?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: The aim of this amendment is to make money available for the larger loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Why is it desired to make more of these larger loans? All these loans are riskier than the ordinary bank loan. As I understand the practice, the only loans made by the Industrial Development Bank are those which the commercial banks cannot or will not make. The applicant for a loan is first interviewed by his bank and then is referred to the Industrial Development Bank. The larger the loan the more chance there is of there being a larger loss. The original act was intended to help the smali man, and I refer the parliamentary assistant to the recital which reads:
Whereas it is desirable to establish an industrial development bank to promote the economic welfare of Canada by increasing the effectiveness of monetary action through ensuring the availability of credit to industrial enterprises which may reasonably be expected to prove successful if a high level of national income and employment is maintained, by supplementing the activities of other lenders and by providing capital assistance to industry with particular consideration to the financing problems of small enterprises:
It seems strange that we are now being asked to provide $10 million more for large loans which will reduce the aggregate available for small loans. I think hon. members who were here in 1944 when the original act was passed will agree that it was intended to help get industry on its feet after the war, particularly to help to get the small man established. It was never intended to be a permanent lending institution down through

the years. But by this bill we are expanding the business in large loans, and restricting the possibility of making the smaller loans. Why is that being done? Is there a greater demand for loans of over $200,000? Why is the bank asking for this particular power which seems to be contrary to the intent of the act as originally passed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: The bank caters particularly to the small-sized industrial enterprises. The individual or company which needs $200,000 for plant expansion is not a particularly large business. A small lumber mill worth $200,000 may want to expand by another $200,000. When it buys a few planing machines and a band saw it will have used up the $200,000 right there. There has been a considerable increase in capital cost since 1944. It has been found that a prospective borrower who could expand his plant for $150,000 in 1944 or 1945 will now need $200,000 or $225,000 to buy the same machinery. That is why the bank is asking an increase in the limits imposed by the original act.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: It is now being provided that the bank may lend to an individual or company where somebody else has invested money in the enterprise. Under the original act a loan could be made only to a man who was putting in his own money or to a company which had sold its shares to an individual. In other words, the original idea was to help the man or company who had put his or their own money into an undertaking. We are now going a step further and giving power to lend where an investment has been made by others, where there is other money in the business. The Industrial Development Bank will simply be one creditor among one or more other creditors. Why is it necessary to branch out into that type of loan? It will not be as good a loan and I was wondering why the bank wants to branch out in that way. There is one other point which I will raise after the parliamentary assistant answers.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: No, I do not interpret clause 2 in the same way as the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. By "person" I imagine he refers now to section 15, subsection 1, paragraph (c)-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
-which reads:
The amount invested or to be invested in the industrial enterprise by persons other than the bank . . .
The money invested by the owners, being persons other than the bank-

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
No, that is not it. That is the way the act read originally, and of course no

one can quarrel with the original terminology. Here is the explanation given in the explanatory note:
It also permits the bank to make a loan where money has been invested by some other person in the enterprise so long as the board is satisfied that the amount invested by others affords reasonable protection to the bank.
The wording of the new clause (c) is "by persons other than the bank", which means that you can have a second or third creditor. The parliamentary assistant said that in his statement explaining the bill. He also said that the Industrial Development Bank was to get priority over other creditors. I should like to have an explanation as to just what the situation is. I do not understand why the bank should ask for this wider power.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
Of course the bank lends money only on first security to the owners of the enterprise. Section 16 of the original act stipulates that:
The bank may take, accept or acquire and may hold collateral security of any kind and in any form for the repayment of any loan, made or guaranteed by it under this act. and without limiting the generality of the foregoing-
The bank may take stock, bonds, debentures, warehouse receipts and bills of lading, goods, wares and merchandise, mortgages or hypothecs. You have to be the owner of these rights if you want to transfer them as collateral security to the bank.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That does not deal with the case of a second creditor. If the bank is to have the right to loan, where there are other people who have loaned money to the business, then at least there should be a provision written in the clause that the Industrial Development Bank will get priority over these other creditors.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
The hon. member has read the explanatory note, but I think it should be read in conjunction with paragraph (c). The explanatory note reads:
It also permits the bank to make a loan where money has been Invested by some other person-
That is as stipulated in subsection (c), "other than the bank".

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That is not right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: And so long as the bank is satisfied that the amount invested by others than the bank affords reasonable protection to the bank.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
I am very much concerned about this because I am quite sure the parliamentary assistant is not interpreting the amendment correctly. The explanatory note says:
The amendment permits the bank to make credit available if the board is satisfied that the applicant is about to undertake an enterprise and that the enterprise is an industrial enterprise.
Industrial Development Bank Act
That was the effect of the old provision.
It also permits the bank to make a loan where money has been invested by some other person in the enterprise so long as the board is satisfied that the amount invested by others affords reasonable protection to the bank.
The wording of the new section is clearly for that specific purpose. The proposed amendment to section 15 reads, "where in the opinion of the board", and then it sets out certain things. A person must be engaged in an industrial enterprise, credit is not otherwise available, and then paragraph (c) reads:
The amount invested or to be invested in the industrial enterprise by persons other than the bank . . .
They make it broad so that it covers both the man who is in the business and anyone who is lending him money in addition to the Industrial Development Bank. Paragraph (c) goes on to read:
-and the character of that investment are such as to afford the bank reasonable protection.
There may be some good reason why the bank wants that additional power, but why is it trying to make these loans where there are other creditors?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I have had some little experience with these loans. I think it covers the case where a man, a returned soldier we will say, has undertaken to start a small business, has borrowed from his father and his relatives and obtained a sum which he thought was sufficient. It later develops it is not sufficient and he goes to the Industrial Development Bank and asks for help. His business is already mortgaged to his friends, and under the old act the bank could not function. I think this simply gives the bank freedom to take security in that kind of situation.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Would the bank get prior security?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I think so. Of course it would be a matter for the bank to arrange, but generally speaking in a situation of that kind, as my hon. friend knows, the last man in gets the preferred position.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
I have one question I wish to ask the parliamentary assistant. In the original section 2 of the act the definition of "industrial enterprise" is as follows:
"Industrial enterprise" means a business in which the manufacture, processing or refrigeration of goods, wares and merchandise or the building, alteration or repair of ships or vessels or the generating or distributing of electricity is carried on.
Can a co-operative qualify as an industrial enterprise for the purpose of carrying on these various businesses, and if they can how many loans have been made to co-operatives for this purpose?

Industrial Development Bank Act

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I think a co-operative can obtain a loan if it is an industrial enterprise according to the definition.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: And incorporated; it would have to be incorporated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: It has to have some kind of incorporation or registration.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Is there a branch of this bank in the three prairie provinces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Yes, there is a branch in Winnipeg.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I think it is my turn now.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. As the hon. member knows, the Chair must see members of various parties.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: You saw me before sufficiently to make me sit down.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Order. I saw the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra. Then I proceeded to see the hon. member for Mel-fort who rose before you. Now I proceed to give the floor to the senior member for Halifax.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I shall be very brief. If the hon. member for Queens will be patient, I will not keep him waiting very long. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant about the definition of "industrial enterprise". In order to make it a little clearer, I have in mind an operator of fishing vessels which fish in the far north. They are manned by sailors from Newfoundland and the other maritime provinces, and because of the sealing industry they produce oil. To our way of thinking the production of this oil is an industry, but up to the present time there has not been a clear-cut interpretation, so those who would like to borrow money either for the purchase of fishing boats or for the overhauling of machinery have not been able to do so. I feel there should be a clearer interpretation of the term "industrial enterprise" than we have had up to the present. While I am on my feet may I add that because we do not have a representative closer to the maritimes than Montreal it is rather difficult to get the interpretations that we would sometimes like to have.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I am informed that fishing enterprises of the kind which have been described by the senior member for Halifax have obtained loans.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That is fine; then I shall be safe in telling those who have made application that their loans will be granted, so those who are fishing or sealing in the far north not only will be able to carry on those enterprises but will be able to make any necessary alterations to their ships.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Is the Industrial Development Bank a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That is correct.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Then is that why Prince Edward Island has not been able to get any loans through the industrial bank following the withdrawal of the Bank of Canada from that province? Where is there a branch of the industrial bank in the maritime provinces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: There is no branch of the bank in Prince Edward Island, but money has been loaned in that province.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I want to get this straight. Is the Industrial Development Bank a subsidiary of the Bank of Canada?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: It was organized as such.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: I want to ask if the Industrial Development Bank has an office anywhere in the maritimes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: No, sir; not in the maritimes. The Montreal office serves the Atlantic division.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: As usual everything east of Toronto is written off. What is the function of the Industrial Development Bank? Is it to help create new industries, or just to assist in the expansion of existing industries?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Both.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
I ask that question because I had occasion to make some inquiries about a year ago. I know quite a number of applications were made by people such as those described by the parliamentary assistant, people who wanted to put a little capital into a small industry; but none of those applications were granted. I received letters asking me to find out why that was so, and my inquiries revealed this. I was told by an official that the bank was not created for the purpose of assisting in the establishment of new industries but rather to assist in the expansion of existing industries. I asked specifically why the loans in which I was interested had been rejected. The answer was that the people applying did not have sufficient credit. I asked what credit was necessary, and was told that if they could go to a bank and have the bank sponsor them for $10,000, $15,000 or $20,000, if they had the collateral to support that kind of loan and got the endorsation of a bank, they could get a loan from the Industrial Development Bank. Well, if they had that kind of credit they did not need the Industrial Development Bank.
Personally I do not think it serves any purpose. I was in the house when this bank was set up, and this group supported it as a move in the right direction. We were led to believe that it was to provide the kind of credit that

A'ould not be provided through the chartered banks, that it would make funds available for the establishment of small industries where the persons concerned did not have the necessary bank credit to carry out the undertaking. I was quite satisfied that it was a step in the right direction. I visualized many small industries springing up in the maritime provinces, but when I made inquiries the information I obtained was that it was not intended for that purpose; so I do not know just what purpose it does serve. Certainly it serves no purpose in the maritime provinces. It does not even have an office there; if you want to make contact at all you must write to Montreal. If this is part of the national bank I think there should be an office or a representative in each province.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Under the act as it stood, and as it is amended, the words "the bank may lend or guarantee loans" appear. Can the parliamentary assistant tell us, as at any stage, how much of the money the bank has out is from the funds of the bank itself, and how much is by way of guarantee?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: The bank authorizes a credit but does not disburse it immediately. Let us say it authorizes a credit of $100,000 to build or enlarge a plant. The bank does not disburse the $100,000 right away, but only as the work progresses.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: That is interesting, but I do not think it quite answers my question. From this wording I understand that the bank may make or guarantee loans. Does that mean that, in some cases, on the basis of the bank's guarantee the borrower goes to some other institution, say a chartered bank, and borrows the money?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext:
No. After having authorized a credit the Industrial Development Bank could endorse a note.
Industrial Development Bank Act

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: We are getting close to an answer now. What percentage of the liabilities of the bank-or is it assets?-are in the form of these guaranteed notes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: AMENDMENTS WITH RESPECT TO LOANS, EXPENDITURES, ETC.
speechtext: Looking at the reports I do not think there are any such guarantees.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the bill was given second reading only this evening, and many hon. members were not here. I suggest that it should not be put through two readings in the same day, except by unanimous consent.
